title: Android Scopes & Lifecycle
scopeHtml: Scope: viewModelScope and lifecycleScope internals, launchWhenX deprecation, an overview of repeatOnLifecycle, GlobalScope, an application scope through Hilt, save-on-leave, CoroutineWorker and WorkManager, LifecycleService, viewLifecycleOwner, and process death. Deep flow-collection mechanics (stateIn, WhileSubscribed, collectAsStateWithLifecycle) live in the F5 chunk. Job and SupervisorJob semantics live in C4, and exception handling lives in C6.

notes.title: viewModelScope basics and internals
notes.html:
The idea, simply. viewModelScope is a ready-made coroutine scope that belongs to a ViewModel. When the screen is really gone (not just rotated), the ViewModel is cleared and every coroutine you launched in it is cancelled automatically. It is "free cleanup".

What it is made of. SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate.

  • SupervisorJob: one failed child does not cancel the other children (but an uncaught exception still crashes the app).
  • Dispatchers.Main.immediate: runs on the main thread (details in the next section).

How it is wired (lifecycle-viewmodel-ktx; names are from the library source, check your version). The extension property ViewModel.viewModelScope looks up a tag (JOB_KEY = "androidx.lifecycle.ViewModelCoroutineScope.JOB_KEY") stored inside the ViewModel; if missing it creates a CloseableCoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate) and stores it with setTagIfAbsent. CloseableCoroutineScope implements Closeable, and its close() calls coroutineContext.cancel().

What happens at clearing. When the ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity finished / Fragment removed / nav back stack entry popped) clears its ViewModelStore, each ViewModel's clear() runs: it closes all closeables (the scope is one of them, plus any you register), then calls onCleared(). In Lifecycle 2.5+ you can register your own: addCloseable(...) or pass closeables to the constructor, and Hilt/other libraries use this to tie resources to the ViewModel. This is not called on process death or configuration change (rotation keeps the ViewModel).

Use after clear. Launching in viewModelScope after onCleared() returns a cancelled coroutine (it never runs). In onCleared() itself, viewModelScope is already cancelled, so you cannot launch "final save" work there (the spot-the-bug case): use an application-scope or WorkManager for must-finish work, or save earlier (onStop).

class FeedViewModel(private val repo: FeedRepo) : ViewModel() {
    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch { _state.value = repo.load() }
    override fun onCleared() {
        viewModelScope.launch { repo.saveDraft() }   // BUG: scope already cancelled, never runs
    }
}

Industry examples. Every MVVM Android app (Google I/O app, Now in Android, Reddit, Spotify); Hilt @HiltViewModel; Paging's cachedIn(viewModelScope) which ties the paging pipeline to the ViewModel.

Real-life picture. A hotel room key card that stops working the instant you check out: everything you started in the room is cleaned up with it.

Common interview traps.

  • Launching "final" work in onCleared().
  • Thinking viewModelScope is cancelled on rotation (it is not).
  • Believing viewModelScope is lifecycle-aware of STARTED/STOPPED (it only knows "alive or cleared").
  • Believing SupervisorJob stops crashes.

notes.title: lifecycleScope and Main immediate
notes.html:
lifecycleScope. Available on any LifecycleOwner (Activity, Fragment, viewLifecycleOwner). It is SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate, and it is cancelled when the lifecycle reaches DESTROYED (implemented by LifecycleCoroutineScopeImpl registering a lifecycle observer). Launching when the lifecycle is already DESTROYED gives an immediately cancelled coroutine. It does not pause when the screen is in the background (STOPPED): a lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect {} } keeps collecting while the app is invisible.

Main.immediate vs Main.

  • Dispatchers.Main always posts to the main thread's Handler (even when already on it); the code runs on the next loop iteration.
  • Dispatchers.Main.immediate checks "am I already on the main thread?" (Looper.myLooper() == Looper.getMainLooper()) and if so runs the block immediately (inline) until its first suspension.

Why scopes use immediate: state updates happen without a frame of delay, avoiding flicker and unnecessary posting. Subtle effects: (1) the code before the first suspension runs synchronously inside your launch call (re-entrancy: a callback may run while you are still inside the calling function); (2) ordering differs from Dispatchers.Main (the immediate block runs before other already-posted messages); (3) tests need Dispatchers.setMain(...); (4) a deep chain of immediate resumptions is limited with an unconfined-style event loop, so there is no stack overflow.

Log.d("T", "before")
lifecycleScope.launch { Log.d("T", "inside") }   // prints inside right here (on the main thread)
Log.d("T", "after")
// With Dispatchers.Main (not immediate): before, after, inside

Real-life picture. Main is giving your note to the receptionist who puts it at the back of the queue; Main.immediate is walking into the office you are already standing in.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming launch on Main always defers the block.
  • Collecting flows in lifecycleScope.launch and expecting them to stop in the background.
  • Forgetting Dispatchers.setMain in unit tests.

notes.title: repeatOnLifecycle and launchWhenX
notes.html:
The problem. UI should collect flows only while visible (STARTED). lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect {} } keeps collecting in the background: wasted battery, location/sensor updates alive, and updates to views that are not visible.

repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { } (lifecycle-runtime-ktx 2.4.0+). A suspend function. Each time the lifecycle reaches STARTED, it launches your block in a new coroutine; when it falls below STARTED (onStop) it cancels that coroutine; when it returns to STARTED it launches it again. It returns only when the lifecycle is DESTROYED.

viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        launch { vm.state.collect(::render) }       // each flow needs its own launch
        launch { vm.events.collect(::handle) }      // collect never returns
    }
}

Single-flow shortcut: flow.flowWithLifecycle(lifecycle, STARTED).onEach{}.launchIn(lifecycleScope). Compose: collectAsStateWithLifecycle() (lifecycle-runtime-compose).

launchWhenStarted / launchWhenResumed (deprecated since Lifecycle 2.6). They suspend the coroutine when the lifecycle is below the state but do not cancel it. The upstream producer keeps running (a callbackFlow keeps its location listener, a Flow keeps hitting the network), only the collector's dispatcher is paused, which buffers or backs up emissions. Also a dangerous pattern was launchWhenX { coroutine does non-UI work } which stalls work forever when stopped.

Migration (live traffic). Search the code base for launchWhenStarted|launchWhenResumed|launchWhenCreated|whenStarted; replace flow collection with repeatOnLifecycle; verify that the screen does a refresh/restart on returning (collection now restarts, so stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5_000)) keeps hot flows warm across short stops like rotation); watch: duplicate event handling (events replayed from a SharedFlow with replay), one-shot events lost when stopped (use Channel + receiveAsFlow or state-based events), and metrics for battery/network. Roll out behind a flag per screen, compare Crashlytics, Firebase Performance and background network usage.

Industry examples. Google's recommended pattern since the 2021 Android Developers "A safer way to collect flows" article; Now in Android uses collectAsStateWithLifecycle.

Real-life picture. launchWhenStarted is pausing a TV show but leaving the recorder running; repeatOnLifecycle is switching the recorder off and starting a new recording when you come back.

Common interview traps.

  • Using lifecycleScope.launch { collect } for UI flows.
  • Putting two collect calls sequentially inside repeatOnLifecycle (the second never runs).
  • Believing launchWhenStarted cancels the upstream.
  • Assuming repeatOnLifecycle returns before DESTROYED.

notes.title: Fragment viewLifecycleOwner
notes.html:
The problem. A Fragment instance can outlive its view: on the back stack, onDestroyView() runs but the Fragment (and its lifecycleScope) stays alive. If you collect flows or observe LiveData using the Fragment's lifecycle (this/lifecycleScope), then:

  • when the user returns, onViewCreated runs again and you register a second collector while the first is still active: duplicate UI updates, double navigation, double toasts;
  • the old collector holds the destroyed view (binding) = a view leak, and may touch it after onDestroyView (NPE / IllegalStateException, or "binding is null").

Fix. Use viewLifecycleOwner for anything touching views: viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope, viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle, liveData.observe(viewLifecycleOwner). viewLifecycleOwner is created in onCreateView and destroyed in onDestroyView. Calling viewLifecycleOwner before the view exists (e.g. in onCreate) throws IllegalStateException; use viewLifecycleOwnerLiveData if needed. Use the Fragment's own lifecycleScope for non-UI work tied to the Fragment instance.

override fun onViewCreated(v: View, s: Bundle?) {
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { vm.state.collect(::render) }
    }
}

Detection. LeakCanary reports "Fragment.mView / binding leaked", Android lint has a check for LiveData observe in onCreateView with this.

Real-life picture. Hiring a new waiter every time a customer re-enters the restaurant without releasing the old one: everyone shouts the same order.

Common interview traps.

  • Observing LiveData with this in onViewCreated (lint warns).
  • Using Fragment lifecycleScope for view updates.
  • Keeping binding alive after onDestroyView.

notes.title: GlobalScope pitfalls
notes.html:
What it is. GlobalScope is a scope with no Job and Dispatchers.Default. Coroutines launched there are not children of anything: they live until they finish or the process dies. Marked @DelicateCoroutinesApi (compiler warning).

Why it is bad on Android.

  • Never cancelled when the screen goes away: continues network/CPU/battery use.
  • Lambdas capture this/Activity/Fragment/ViewModel => memory leak (heap dumps show StandaloneCoroutine -> Activity).
  • No structure: exceptions go straight to the uncaught handler (crash), no parent to handle or wait.
  • Hard to test (real dispatchers, cannot control time).
  • Work is not durable: the process can still die (use WorkManager when it must survive).

Alternatives. UI-bound work to viewModelScope/lifecycleScope; must-finish short work to an injected application scope; guaranteed work to WorkManager; parent-bound work with coroutineScope { }.

Rare legitimate uses. Truly process-lifetime, top-level, non-capturing tasks (even then, a named application scope is better).

Real-life picture. Giving a worker an open-ended task with no manager, no timetable and no way to call them back.

Common interview traps.

  • Using GlobalScope to "survive rotation" (ViewModel does that).
  • Thinking GlobalScope survives process death.
  • Passing GlobalScope as the default argument in repositories.

notes.title: Work outliving a screen and application scope
notes.html:
The decision table.

Need Tool
Stops when the screen goes (rotation excluded) viewModelScope
Stops when the view/UI is gone viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope + repeatOnLifecycle
Must finish even if the user leaves, but process stays alive (send message, submit payment confirmation) injected application scope
Must finish even if process dies / device reboots / needs constraints (upload KYC photo, sync) WorkManager
User-visible ongoing task (music, navigation) foreground service (+ its own scope)

Application scope via Hilt.

@Qualifier annotation class ApplicationScope
@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object ScopeModule {
    @Provides @Singleton @ApplicationScope
    fun appScope(@DefaultDispatcher d: CoroutineDispatcher) =
        CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + d + CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Crashlytics.log(e) })
}

Inject it into repositories that need "launch and don't cancel with the screen". It must have a SupervisorJob, a handler, an injectable dispatcher (tests), and must never capture Activities/Views.

Application scope leaks (incident). An @Singleton scope launching a coroutine that captured a ViewModel/Activity lambda (callback in a loop, collect of a never-ending flow, delay(Long.MAX)-style waiters) retains it for the whole process life: LeakCanary shows the singleton -> scope -> coroutine -> Activity chain; heap grows with every screen open. Also unbounded jobs accumulate (polling started on every screen entry and never cancelled). Fix: store only application-lifetime data in lambdas, pass IDs not Contexts, keep a Job reference and cancel/replace it, and prefer distinctUntilChanged + stateIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed) for shared hot data.

Polling scope placement (design). Poll while the screen is visible: repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) + while(isActive) { fetch(); delay(15s) } inside the UI or a flow in the ViewModel with WhileSubscribed(5_000) (stops 5 s after the last collector leaves, surviving rotation). Poll only while logged in: session scope. Poll even in background: not with coroutines, use push (FCM) or WorkManager periodic work (min 15 min).

lifecycleScope work across rotation (ambiguous requirement). Rotation destroys the Activity, so lifecycleScope is cancelled and restarted; an in-flight upload started there dies. Move it into the ViewModel (survives rotation) if it should continue while the screen lives, or to application scope/WorkManager if it must survive leaving. Clarify the requirement: "survive rotation", "survive back", or "survive process death".

Post-event review in a nutshell. Ask for each coroutine: who owns it, when is it cancelled, what does it capture, what happens at rotation, back, kill, logout.

Real-life picture. Some errands are for the household (application scope), some only while the guest is visiting (screen), and some you give to a courier company because you may be unavailable (WorkManager).

Common interview traps.

  • Using the application scope as a replacement for ViewModel scope.
  • Application scope without handler/SupervisorJob.
  • Treating an app scope as durable; the process may die.
  • Starting a poller on each onCreate without cancelling the previous one.

notes.title: CoroutineWorker basics and stop semantics
notes.html:
What it is. CoroutineWorker (work-runtime-ktx / work-runtime 2.x) is a Worker whose doWork() is a suspend fun. WorkManager starts a coroutine on Dispatchers.Default (override coroutineContext property to change), calls doWork(), and maps the returned Result.success()/failure()/retry().

class SyncWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result = try {
        repo.sync(); Result.success()
    } catch (e: IOException) { Result.retry() }
}

Stop and cancellation semantics. When WorkManager stops a worker (constraints no longer met, the work is cancelled by you, a new unique work replaces it with REPLACE, the system decides to stop it, or the time limit hits), the worker's coroutine is cancelled (CancellationException at the next cancellation point), and onStopped() is called. Whatever result you return after being stopped is ignored; the work is rescheduled according to its state (e.g. retried when stopped by constraints/system). So:

  • Do not swallow CancellationException in doWork.
  • Make work idempotent and resumable (checkpoint progress in Room/setProgress), because it can be stopped at any point and run again.
  • Use finally with NonCancellable for essential cleanup, kept short.
  • Time limit: about 10 minutes of execution for a regular worker (confirm in docs for your version), and Android can stop it earlier. For long jobs use setForeground(ForegroundInfo) (foreground service type; expedited work on Android 12+ has quotas), or break work into chunks.
  • Newer WorkManager exposes stopReason (getStopReason(), confirm version) to see why it was stopped.

WorkManager vs scopes cost (cost/perf). A coroutine in viewModelScope/app scope costs hundreds of bytes and microseconds, but is lost if the process dies; WorkManager costs more (a Room database of work specs, JobScheduler/AlarmManager integration, a process wake-up, ~tens of ms to schedule, system-imposed delays under Doze/standby buckets) but guarantees execution. Use WorkManager for deferrable guaranteed work (not for work that must run now and is cheap/retryable by UI, like a refresh on screen entry). Overusing WorkManager for "tiny immediate" tasks (analytics events one by one) causes many wake-ups and backlog; batch instead.

Industry examples. Instagram/WhatsApp-like uploads via WorkManager with network constraints; Firebase's background syncing; Google Photos backup using foreground workers.

Real-life picture. A courier company: you hand over the parcel, and they promise to deliver it eventually, even if you go on holiday; but they may stop at night and resume the next day, so the delivery process must be restartable.

Common interview traps.

  • Returning Result.success() from a catch (Exception) that ate cancellation.
  • Not making work idempotent.
  • Assuming a worker can run unlimited time.
  • Using WorkManager for something needed immediately.

notes.title: LifecycleService and coroutines in services
notes.html:
The idea. A Service has no built-in coroutine scope. Use LifecycleService (lifecycle-service artifact) to get lifecycleScope, cancelled when the service is destroyed, or build your own CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) and cancel() it in onDestroy().

Mechanics and rules.

  • Cancel the scope in onDestroy(); otherwise coroutines outlive the service (leak of service context).
  • A started service in the background is limited (API 26+ background execution limits); a foreground service must call startForeground() within a few seconds (about 5 s) of startForegroundService() or the system throws ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException/ANR-style crash; Android 12+ restricts starting foreground services from the background (ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException); Android 14 requires a foreground service type.
  • onStartCommand runs on the main thread: launch coroutines for work; call stopSelf() when the work completes, and use stopSelf(startId) to avoid stopping while newer commands arrive.
  • Service scope, like any scope, dies with the process: for guaranteed work use WorkManager.
  • lifecycleScope in LifecycleService follows onCreate -> onDestroy of the service, not any activity.

Industry examples. Music players (Spotify, YouTube Music) run a MediaSessionService/foreground service with its own scope; navigation apps like Google Maps use foreground services for turn-by-turn tracking.

Real-life picture. A shop's night-shift staff who go home when the shop closes (onDestroy), unless the manager forgets to dismiss them.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to cancel a custom scope in onDestroy.
  • Missing startForeground deadlines.
  • Assuming services survive process death.

notes.title: Process death and save-on-leave patterns
notes.html:
What process death does. When Android kills your process (low memory while in the background, "Don't keep activities", swipe away from Recents, crash), everything in memory disappears at once: all coroutines, ViewModels, singletons. No finally, no onCleared(), no onDestroy() is guaranteed to run. After the user returns, the system recreates the Activity with savedInstanceState, but your ViewModel is new.

Implications.

  • A coroutine-based "save later" is never guaranteed: work in memory is lost.
  • Anything the user must not lose must be persisted before the process can die (when going to the background) or be handed to WorkManager.
  • Restore UI state from SavedStateHandle (small, via Bundle limit ~ 1 MB total across the transaction, keep it tiny) plus Room/DataStore for real data.

Save-on-leave patterns.

  1. Debounced autosave while the user edits (e.g. 500 ms after the last keystroke: Gmail/Notion-style drafts) so little is lost at any time.
  2. Save on onStop (the last callback guaranteed on all API levels before the process may be killed; onSaveInstanceState is called after onStop on API 28+). Do a short, fast persist, with fire-and-forget into the application scope or a WorkManager enqueue.
  3. onCleared/onDestroy are unreliable (and viewModelScope is already cancelled there).
  4. Write-ahead: write the intent to a local "outbox" table in a Room transaction, then process the outbox with WorkManager (WhatsApp/Telegram-style outgoing messages).
  5. Idempotent processing with a client-generated ID so a retry after death does not duplicate.

Post-incident review of a scope-owned job. A checkout confirmation was launched in viewModelScope while the user pressed Home; the OS killed the process; the order was charged but never confirmed with the server. Root cause: durable intent stored only in memory and a scope whose lifetime was the screen. Fix: persist intent in Room, process via WorkManager with an idempotency key, show pending state on restore, add reconciliation job.

Real-life picture. Writing in pencil on a whiteboard that can be wiped any time: copy the important notes into a notebook as you go.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on onCleared/onDestroy to save.
  • Storing large data in SavedStateHandle/Bundle (TransactionTooLargeException).
  • Testing only rotation, not "Don't keep activities"/adb shell am kill process death.
  • Assuming an application-scope coroutine is durable.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• viewModelScope = SupervisorJob + Main.immediate, cancelled by ViewModel.clear() (closeable) before onCleared runs; survives rotation, not process death.
  • lifecycleScope is cancelled at DESTROYED, not paused in the background; use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) (cancels and restarts) instead of the deprecated launchWhenX (suspends but leaves upstream active).
  • In Fragments, view-related work belongs to viewLifecycleOwner.
  • Main.immediate runs inline when already on the main thread, Main always posts.
  • GlobalScope has no lifecycle, leaks, crashes uncontrolled; prefer proper scopes.
  • Work that must outlive a screen goes to an injected application scope (with SupervisorJob and handler) or to WorkManager when it must survive process death.
  • CoroutineWorker is cancelled on stop: be cancellation-friendly, idempotent, and mind time limits and foreground info.
  • Services need an explicit scope (LifecycleService.lifecycleScope or your own cancelled in onDestroy).
  • Process death wipes coroutines and ViewModels; persist early (debounced autosave, onStop, outbox + WorkManager).

questions.promptHtml: What is viewModelScope, when is it cancelled, and why should most ViewModel coroutines run in it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the entry-level Android coroutines question. They want to hear that a scope's lifetime is tied to an owner, and that a ViewModel outlives configuration changes but not leaving the screen.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: viewModelScope is a CoroutineScope extension property on ViewModel. It's created lazily the first time you touch it, and it's cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared, right before onCleared() runs. A ViewModel is cleared when its ViewModelStoreOwner goes away for good: the Activity finishes, the Fragment is removed, or the navigation back-stack entry is popped. It is not cleared on rotation. So anything launched there survives configuration changes and dies when the user leaves the screen. That's exactly the lifetime of "load data for this screen", so I don't have to cancel anything by hand.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A coroutine always needs a scope, which gives it a Job to hang off and a default dispatcher. The question is who owns the cancellation. Before lifecycle-viewmodel-ktx, people created val job = Job() in the ViewModel and called job.cancel() in onCleared(), and forgetting it leaked work. viewModelScope bakes that pattern into the library.

Activity created ─▶ ViewModelProvider gets/creates VM ─▶ VM in ViewModelStore
     │ rotate: Activity destroyed + recreated, ViewModelStore retained ─▶ same VM, scope alive
     │ user presses back / finish(): isChangingConfigurations == false
     ▼
ViewModelStore.clear() ─▶ vm.clear() ─▶ closeables closed (viewModelScope cancelled) ─▶ onCleared()

When the scope is cancelled, every child coroutine gets a CancellationException at its next suspension point. Retrofit suspend calls cancel the underlying OkHttp Call, and Room queries stop waiting. Work that doesn't suspend keeps running until it checks for cancellation (see the cancellation chunk).

Where it lives: historically lifecycle-viewmodel-ktx. Since lifecycle 2.8 the Kotlin extensions were folded into the base lifecycle-viewmodel artifact as part of the Kotlin Multiplatform work. The -ktx artifact still exists, so either dependency works.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: ProfileRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<ProfileUiState>(ProfileUiState.Loading)
    val state: StateFlow<ProfileUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {                    // survives rotation, cancelled when screen is gone
            _state.value = try {
                ProfileUiState.Loaded(repo.load())
            } catch (e: IOException) {             // narrow catch: CancellationException still propagates
                ProfileUiState.Error(e)
            }
        }
    }
}

// Broken: hand-rolled scope that nobody cancels
class LeakyViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) // never cancelled, outlives the VM
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking viewModelScope is cancelled on rotation. It isn't, and that's the whole point.
  • Assuming it runs on a background thread. It runs on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, and main-safe suspend APIs or withContext handle the thread hop.
  • Using it for work that must finish even when the user leaves, such as an upload or a "save" (see Q412 and Q421).
  • Creating a parallel CoroutineScope(...) field in the ViewModel and never cancelling it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the ViewModel is scoped to a nav graph? → The scope lives until that graph's back-stack entry is popped, which can be several screens.
  2. Can I use it from a plain class? → No. It's an extension on ViewModel. Other classes get a scope injected, or are suspend and let the caller own the scope.
  3. What happens if I touch viewModelScope after onCleared()? → Since lifecycle 2.7, addCloseable on a cleared ViewModel closes the resource immediately. Even before that, the existing scope was already cancelled. Either way, anything launched there is cancelled before it starts (see Q423).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "it cancels when the ViewModel is destroyed". The senior answer says what "cleared" means for each owner type (Activity, Fragment, NavBackStackEntry), explains that cancellation is cooperative, and names which work does not belong there.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team saw "draft lost" bug reports because the save ran in viewModelScope and the user backed out mid-write. The scope was cancelled with the screen, exactly as designed.

questions.promptHtml: What is lifecycleScope, when does it get cancelled, and how is it different in an Activity versus a Fragment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know that lifecycleScope is tied to DESTROYED, not to visibility, and that the Fragment version doesn't follow the view.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: lifecycleScope is lifecycle.coroutineScope on any LifecycleOwner. It uses SupervisorJob() plus Dispatchers.Main.immediate, and it's cancelled when the lifecycle reaches DESTROYED. It does nothing on STOPPED: coroutines keep running in the background. In an Activity, DESTROYED also happens on every rotation, so lifecycleScope work restarts on config change. In a Fragment, lifecycleScope follows the Fragment instance, which outlives its view when the fragment goes onto the back stack. For anything touching views I use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Internally, Lifecycle.coroutineScope lazily creates a LifecycleCoroutineScopeImpl, caches it on the Lifecycle, and registers a LifecycleEventObserver on the main thread. When the observer sees the state drop to DESTROYED, it removes itself and cancels the scope's job. If the lifecycle is already DESTROYED when the scope is created, it cancels immediately.

Owner Scope cancelled when Survives rotation? Survives going to back stack?
Activity lifecycleScope Activity onDestroy No n/a
Fragment lifecycleScope Fragment onDestroy No Yes, while the view is destroyed
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope onDestroyView No No
viewModelScope ViewModel cleared Yes Yes, until popped

The key misconception: "lifecycle-aware" here means aware of destruction only. A lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect { ... } } keeps collecting while the app is in the background. Stopping in the background is what repeatOnLifecycle adds (Q410).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DetailActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            // Runs until onDestroy, including while the app is backgrounded.
            // Restarts from scratch after every rotation.
            delay(3_000)
            showRatingPrompt()
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing lifecycleScope pauses or cancels on onStop. It doesn't.
  • Starting a network load in an Activity's lifecycleScope. It's cancelled and repeated on each rotation, so it belongs in the ViewModel.
  • Using a Fragment's lifecycleScope to update views, which crashes or leaks after onDestroyView (Q411).
  • Using lifecycleScope in a non-UI component that has no real lifecycle (Q416 covers LifecycleService).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which dispatcher does it use? → Dispatchers.Main.immediate, so code launched from the main thread starts synchronously (Q407).
  2. Does a crash in one child cancel the scope? → No, it uses a SupervisorJob. But an uncaught exception still goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler and crashes the app (see the exception chunk).
  3. What does LifecycleCoroutineScope add? → The deprecated launchWhenCreated/Started/Resumed helpers (Q409). Otherwise it's an ordinary scope.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "it's cancelled when the Activity is destroyed". The senior answer adds that it keeps running while the app is backgrounded, that it restarts on rotation, and that a Fragment needs the view lifecycle, and then puts the right work in the right scope.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "show tooltip after 3 s" coroutine in an Activity lifecycleScope fired while the app was in the background, after the user had switched apps. The tooltip was a DialogFragment, so showing it after state was saved crashed with IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState. The fix was repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED).

questions.promptHtml: Why is GlobalScope discouraged on Android, and what does the @DelicateCoroutinesApi annotation tell you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: GlobalScope usage is a code-review red flag. They want to hear the structured-concurrency argument, plus a sensible alternative for real "app-lifetime" work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: GlobalScope has no Job. Coroutines launched there have no parent, so nothing cancels them, nothing waits for them, and failures don't propagate to anyone who cares. That breaks structured concurrency: leaks are invisible, tests can't control them, and a coroutine capturing an Activity lives as long as it runs. Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.5 it's marked @DelicateCoroutinesApi, so you get a warning unless you opt in. If I really need app-lifetime work, I inject an application CoroutineScope with a SupervisorJob, so it's at least owned, injectable and replaceable in tests.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
GlobalScope.coroutineContext is EmptyCoroutineContext. So:

  • No parent Job. Each launch creates a root coroutine. cancel() on GlobalScope throws, because there's no Job to cancel.
  • Default dispatcher. With no dispatcher specified, it runs on Dispatchers.Default, not Main. People are surprised when a UI update from GlobalScope.launch {} crashes with CalledFromWrongThreadException.
  • Exceptions. An uncaught exception in a root launch goes to the global handler, which on Android means a crash. A root async that's never awaited silently drops its exception.
  • Testing. runTest can't see or advance these coroutines unless you swap dispatchers, so tests leak work into each other.
viewModelScope ─┬─ child A          GlobalScope ── A (orphan)
                └─ child B                        ── B (orphan)
cancel() kills both                 no handle, no cancel, no join

What is legitimately "global"? Very little: a process-wide fire-and-forget that's fine to lose on process death. Even then, an injected @ApplicationScope is better (Q413).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bad: orphan coroutine; captures `activity`, runs on Default, untestable
@OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class)
fun onClick(activity: Activity) {
    GlobalScope.launch {
        val user = api.fetchUser()
        activity.title = user.name    // wrong thread + leak
    }
}

// Better: owned scope, injectable
class AnalyticsUploader @Inject constructor(
    @ApplicationScope private val appScope: CoroutineScope
) {
    fun flushLater() { appScope.launch { flush() } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Silencing the warning with @OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class) instead of fixing the design.
  • Replacing GlobalScope with CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) created inline at the call site. That's the same orphan with extra steps.
  • Assuming GlobalScope work survives process death. Nothing in memory does (Q417).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is GlobalScope ever acceptable? → In main() demos and short top-level tools, yes. In app code, an injected application scope is strictly better.
  2. What's the difference between GlobalScope and CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob()) held in a singleton? → The latter has a Job, so you can cancel it, inspect its children, swap it in tests, and attach a CoroutineExceptionHandler.
  3. How would you find all GlobalScope usages in a big codebase? → The compiler warning, plus a Detekt rule (GlobalCoroutineUsage in the coroutines rule set) set to fail the build.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "it can leak". The senior answer names the mechanism (empty context, no parent Job), the Default-dispatcher surprise, the testing cost, and offers the injected application-scope replacement with a lint gate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A legacy analytics flush in GlobalScope held a reference to a destroyed Activity for the length of a 30 s retry loop. LeakCanary flagged it on every rotation during a slow-network test pass.

questions.promptHtml: How is viewModelScope actually implemented? Walk me through its context, how it's created, and how it gets cancelled.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Knowing the implementation explains the behavior: why a child failure doesn't kill siblings, why launch runs immediately, and how lifecycle 2.8 made it overridable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It's a CloseableCoroutineScope whose context is SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate. It's created lazily on first access and stored in the ViewModel under a fixed key as an AutoCloseable. When the ViewModel is cleared, its closeables are closed, and closing the scope calls coroutineContext.cancel(). That runs before onCleared(). Since lifecycle 2.8 you can pass your own scope to the ViewModel(viewModelScope) constructor, which is how I inject a test scope. On KMP targets with no Main dispatcher, the library falls back to EmptyCoroutineContext.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In current AndroidX source (lifecycle 2.8+, viewmodel/internal/CloseableCoroutineScope.kt), creation looks like this:

createViewModelScope():
    dispatcher = try { Dispatchers.Main.immediate }
                 catch (NotImplementedError | IllegalStateException) { EmptyCoroutineContext }
    return CloseableCoroutineScope(dispatcher + SupervisorJob())

CloseableCoroutineScope : AutoCloseable, CoroutineScope
    close() = coroutineContext.cancel()

The viewModelScope getter checks for an existing closeable under VIEW_MODEL_SCOPE_KEY. If there isn't one, it creates the scope and registers it with addCloseable(key, scope). Lifecycle 2.8.0-alpha03 fixed a thread-safety issue in that lazy creation. Older versions (2.1–2.7) did the same thing with the setTagIfAbsent(JOB_KEY, ...) "bag of tags".

Why each piece:

  • SupervisorJob. One failed launch (say, a refresh) shouldn't cancel unrelated siblings like the observing job. Note: the uncaught exception still reaches the thread's handler and crashes the app unless something handles it.
  • Main.immediate. ViewModels mostly mutate UI state. Immediate dispatch avoids a frame of delay and keeps ordering intuitive (Q407).
  • AutoCloseable. It's the same mechanism as addCloseable for any resource, so the scope is just one closeable among many (Q408).

The constructor injection (2.8):

class FeedViewModel(
    repo: FeedRepository,
    scope: CoroutineScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate)
) : ViewModel(scope)

The library wraps the scope you pass with asCloseable() and registers it under the same key, so it's still cancelled on clear. Note that the 2.8.0 release-note snippet writes the default as Dispatchers.Main + SupervisorJob(). That's a CoroutineContext, so wrap it in CoroutineScope(...).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test fun loadsFeed() = runTest {
    val vm = FeedViewModel(FakeRepo(), scope = backgroundScope) // 2.8+: no Dispatchers.setMain needed for vm work
    vm.refresh()
    advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(3, vm.state.value.items.size)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the scope uses Dispatchers.IO or Default. It doesn't.
  • Saying "SupervisorJob means exceptions don't crash". They still crash, but siblings survive.
  • Thinking overriding the scope means you must cancel it yourself. The library still closes it on clear.
  • Forgetting that before 2.8 the only test path was Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher), which is why older codebases have a MainDispatcherRule everywhere.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not Dispatchers.Main without immediate? → It would post every launch to the next looper cycle, even when you're already on main. Ordering surprises and a wasted frame (Q407).
  2. If I pass backgroundScope from runTest, who cancels it? → runTest cancels backgroundScope at the end of the test. The ViewModel clearing would also cancel it.
  3. Is the scope created even if never used? → No. It's lazy, so a ViewModel that never touches it allocates nothing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer names SupervisorJob and Main. The senior answer explains lazy keyed creation, close-before-onCleared ordering, the 2.8 constructor injection and what it changes for testing, and the KMP fallback.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After moving to lifecycle 2.8, one team deleted roughly 200 MainDispatcherRule usages by injecting backgroundScope, and the flaky "Main dispatcher not set" failures went away.

questions.promptHtml: Both viewModelScope and lifecycleScope use Dispatchers.Main.immediate. What does immediate change in practice, and when does it surprise people?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It reveals whether you understand dispatch (posting to a queue) versus inline execution, and the ordering consequences on the main thread.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Dispatchers.Main always posts the coroutine to the main Looper's queue, even if you're already on the main thread. Main.immediate skips the post when you're already on main: isDispatchNeeded returns false, so the coroutine body runs synchronously inside launch up to its first suspension. In Android scopes, a launch from onCreate or a click handler starts right away, and a StateFlow update is visible before the next frame. The surprise is ordering. Code after launch {} runs after the coroutine's first segment, not before it. Re-entrancy can also bite, because nested immediate dispatches use an event loop to avoid stack overflow.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
// On main thread, inside onClick:
println("A")
scope.launch { println("B"); delay(10); println("D") }
println("C")

Dispatchers.Main          : A C B ... D   (B posted to the next looper message)
Dispatchers.Main.immediate: A B C ... D   (B runs inline; it suspends at delay, then returns to C)

After the first suspension, the resumption is dispatched normally. When delay completes, the continuation resumes on main, again immediately if the resumer is already on main.

Why Android chose immediate:

  • No wasted frame. With plain Main, setting UI state inside launch from onCreate would land one looper message later, which can mean one frame showing stale UI.
  • Predictable collect start. Collection started in onStart begins before onResume.

Where it surprises:

  • Ordering assumptions in tests and code. A ViewModel's init { viewModelScope.launch { _state.value = Loading } } runs before the constructor returns. That's usually good, but tests that expect the "initial" value can see Loading instead.
  • Immediate from a background thread. No difference. Dispatch is needed, so it posts.
  • Nested immediate. kotlinx.coroutines guards against unbounded recursion with an event loop for nested immediate/unconfined dispatches, so ordering inside deeply nested synchronous emissions can look odd. Don't rely on it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SearchViewModel : ViewModel() {
    val query = MutableStateFlow("")
    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            query.collect { q -> println("collect $q") } // starts collecting synchronously in init
        }
        query.value = "a"   // collector already subscribed, so it sees "" then "a"
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing immediate means "runs on the current thread no matter what", which is Unconfined. Immediate still guarantees the main thread.
  • Writing UI code that depends on launch being deferred to "after onCreate returns".
  • Overriding the 2.8 constructor with Dispatchers.Main without knowing it changes ordering.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does it differ from Dispatchers.Unconfined? → Unconfined resumes on whatever thread completed the suspension, which could be an OkHttp thread. Immediate always stays on main (see the dispatchers chunk).
  2. Does withContext(Dispatchers.Main.immediate) from main cost a dispatch? → No, it's a no-op switch. That's why main-safe code can call it freely.
  3. In Compose, does rememberCoroutineScope use immediate? → Its default context is the composition's AndroidUiDispatcher, which ties into the frame clock. That's a different mechanism. Don't assume they're identical.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "immediate is faster". The senior answer explains isDispatchNeeded, shows the A-B-C ordering, and names the test and ordering consequences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen flashed an empty state for one frame on low-end devices because a custom ViewModel scope used Dispatchers.Main. Switching to Main.immediate made the cached state render on the first frame.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly happens when a ViewModel is cleared? Explain onCleared, addCloseable, and the ordering guarantees across lifecycle versions.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Teams put cleanup in onCleared and get the order wrong, or try to launch coroutines there. Knowing the clearing contract is a senior-level detail.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ViewModelStore.clear() calls an internal clear() on each ViewModel. That marks the ViewModel cleared, closes every registered AutoCloseable, and then calls onCleared(). viewModelScope is one of those closeables, so by the time onCleared() runs, the scope is already cancelled. Since lifecycle 2.5 I register resources with addCloseable instead of overriding onCleared. 2.7 made addCloseable after clearing close immediately. 2.8 added keyed closeables (addCloseable(key, ...), getCloseable(key)) and switched to AutoCloseable. The order in 2.8 is keyed closeables, then un-keyed ones, then onCleared().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Versioned facts, from the lifecycle release notes:

Version Change
2.5.0 addCloseable(Closeable) and a ViewModel(vararg Closeable) constructor. Resources closed on clear
2.7.0 addCloseable on an already-cleared ViewModel closes the resource immediately
2.8.0 AutoCloseable instead of Closeable. Keyed addCloseable(key, c) and getCloseable(key); reusing a key closes the old resource. ViewModel(viewModelScope: CoroutineScope) constructor. Clear order: keyed, then un-keyed, then onCleared() 
ViewModelStore.clear()
  └─ for each vm: vm.clear()
        isCleared = true
        close keyed closeables       (includes viewModelScope → cancel())
        close un-keyed closeables
        onCleared()                  (scope already cancelled here)

Consequences:

  1. Don't launch in onCleared. It's dead on arrival (Q423).
  2. Cancellation is a signal, not a wait. clear() doesn't wait for coroutines to finish their finally blocks if they suspend. Children are cancelled; any withContext(NonCancellable) cleanup runs afterwards, asynchronously, on Main.
  3. Composition of resources. A repository-owned Closeable (a socket or a CameraX handle) is passed into the ViewModel constructor and cleaned up without boilerplate.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PlayerViewModel(private val player: ExoPlayerHolder) : ViewModel(player) // closed on clear (2.5+)

class SocketViewModel(factory: SocketFactory) : ViewModel() {
    private val socket = factory.open().also { addCloseable(it) } // 2.5+, AutoCloseable since 2.8

    override fun onCleared() {
        // viewModelScope is already cancelled here; do only synchronous cleanup.
        log("cleared")
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• viewModelScope.launch { repo.flush() } inside onCleared(). It never runs.
  • Assuming onCleared runs on rotation. It doesn't, only on final removal.
  • Assuming onCleared runs on process death. It doesn't. The process is killed and no callback runs (Q417).
  • Closing shared singletons through addCloseable on one screen's ViewModel.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. On which thread does clear() run? → Main, from the owner's destruction path (Activity.onDestroy when not changing configurations, or Fragment/NavBackStackEntry teardown).
  2. How do I run a final suspend save when the screen closes? → Hand it to an application scope or WorkManager, not to onCleared (Q418).
  3. What does reusing a key with addCloseable(key, ...) do in 2.8? → It replaces the old resource and closes it immediately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "override onCleared to clean up". The senior answer knows the closeables-first ordering, the version table, that cancellation is asynchronous, and that process death skips all of it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An "end session" analytics event was fired from viewModelScope.launch in onCleared and arrived for 0% of sessions. Nobody noticed for a quarter because the dashboard showed "no data" rather than an error.

questions.promptHtml: launchWhenStarted and the other launchWhenX helpers were deprecated. How did they work, why were they deprecated, and what replaces them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a classic "do you keep up and do you understand why" question. The "why" (pausing versus cancelling) is the real signal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: launchWhenStarted launched in lifecycleScope with a pausing dispatcher. When the lifecycle dropped below STARTED, it didn't cancel the coroutine. It just stopped dispatching it, so the coroutine sat suspended until the lifecycle came back. That's fine for a one-shot delay, but terrible for flows. A callbackFlow producer such as a location listener stays registered, and buffered upstream work keeps running in the background while nobody consumes it. It was deprecated in lifecycle 2.6.0. The replacement is repeatOnLifecycle, which cancels the block when you drop below the state and re-runs it when you return. That's what releases the upstream.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
launchWhenStarted { locationFlow.collect { render(it) } }

STARTED  ──collecting──┐
STOPPED                │ PausingDispatcher queues the resumption: the coroutine is
                       │ suspended, NOT cancelled → callbackFlow's awaitClose never runs →
                       │ the GPS listener stays registered; the buffer fills and then
                       │ backpressures/drops
STARTED  ──resumes with stale buffered value──▶
DESTROYED → cancelled (only now)

repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { locationFlow.collect { render(it) } }
STARTED  ──collecting──
STOPPED  → block cancelled → awaitClose runs → listener unregistered
STARTED  → block re-launched → fresh subscription

Mechanics: whenStateAtLeast wraps the block with a PausingDispatcher driven by a LifecycleController. Below the target state, the controller pauses the dispatch queue. Because the pause happens only at dispatch points, code that's mid-execution (not suspended) finishes its current segment. The lifecycle notes say the deprecation is because the pausing dispatcher can waste resources. It was introduced in 2.6.0-alpha04 and is final in 2.6.0, and the notes point to repeatOnLifecycle.

Replacement mapping:

Old Replacement Note
launchWhenStarted { flow.collect {} } launch { repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { flow.collect {} } } Restartable
launchWhenResumed { oneShotUiAction() } withResumed { } or withStarted { } (lifecycle 2.6+, non-suspending block) Runs once when the state is reached
whenStarted { suspendStuff() } Usually move the logic to the ViewModel, or use repeatOnLifecycle if it must restart

withStarted and its siblings (withCreated/withResumed/withStateAtLeast) take a non-suspending block. They're meant for "run this UI action once the state is reached", like a fragment transaction.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Deprecated (lifecycle 2.6+)
lifecycleScope.launchWhenStarted { viewModel.events.collect(::handle) }

// Replacement
lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.events.collect(::handle)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking launchWhenStarted cancels on stop. It never did.
  • A mechanical find-and-replace with repeatOnLifecycle when the block was one-shot. It now re-runs on every start (Q420).
  • Claiming "it's deprecated because it leaks memory". It wastes resources and keeps upstreams alive. The coroutine is still cancelled at DESTROYED.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Do events behave differently after migrating? → Yes. With launchWhenStarted, the collector stays subscribed while paused, so a default MutableSharedFlow() (no buffer) suspends the emitter until the collector resumes: upstream is backpressured and nothing is dropped. With repeatOnLifecycle, there's no subscriber while stopped, so a no-replay SharedFlow drops those emissions. It's the same code with different delivery semantics (one-off event design is covered in F2b).
  2. Why not just add cancellation to launchWhenX? → That changes semantics for existing callers. A new API with explicit restart semantics was cleaner.
  3. What did addRepeatingJob do? → An early alpha API removed in 2.4.0-alpha02 in favor of the suspending repeatOnLifecycle. It's trivia, but shows you followed the design.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "use repeatOnLifecycle instead". The senior answer explains pause versus cancel at the dispatcher level, the callbackFlow/awaitClose consequence, the version, and the one-shot replacement (withStarted), and warns that migration changes restart semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Battery reports showed GPS active for hours in the background on a maps screen. The collector used launchWhenStarted, so the callbackFlow never reached awaitClose. Moving to repeatOnLifecycle dropped background location time to near zero.

questions.promptHtml: What does repeatOnLifecycle do, why is it a suspend function, and where should you call it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the modern answer to "collect safely in the UI". They check that you know it's restartable, that it suspends the caller, and where it goes. Deep stateIn/WhileSubscribed interplay belongs to the F5 chunk.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(state) { ... } launches the block in a new coroutine each time the lifecycle reaches state. It cancels that coroutine when the lifecycle drops below state, and returns only when the lifecycle is DESTROYED. Because it suspends until destruction, nothing after it in the same coroutine runs while the UI is alive. So I put each independent collector in its own launch inside the block. I call it once from onCreate (Activity) or onViewCreated with viewLifecycleOwner (Fragment), never from onStart/onResume, which would stack a new repeater on every start. It's been stable since lifecycle 2.4.0.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
lifecycleScope.launch {                      // outer coroutine, lives until DESTROYED
    repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) {             // suspends here
        // inner coroutine #1: ON_START → ON_STOP (cancelled)
        // inner coroutine #2: next ON_START → ON_STOP
    }
    // reached only after DESTROYED, which in practice never matters
}

Mechanics, simplified: it registers a LifecycleEventObserver. On the "up" event for the state (ON_START for STARTED), it launches the block in a child of the calling coroutine. On the matching "down" event (ON_STOP), it cancels that child. On ON_DESTROY, it resumes the suspended caller. Since 2.4.0-alpha03 the block runs serially: a new run doesn't start until the previous cancelled run has finished. Passing Lifecycle.State.INITIALIZED throws IllegalArgumentException. If the lifecycle is already DESTROYED, it returns immediately.

Why cancel-and-restart is what you want: cancellation travels upstream, so callbackFlow producers reach awaitClose, and stateIn(WhileSubscribed(...)) sees the subscriber count drop. That's how background work actually stops (details in F5).

flowWithLifecycle(lifecycle, state) is the single-flow convenience built on the same mechanism. Lint check RepeatOnLifecycleWrongUsage (added in 2.4.0-alpha02) flags calls from onStart/onResume.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            launch { viewModel.uiState.collect(::render) }
            launch { viewModel.events.collect(::handleEvent) }
        }
    }
}

// Bug: the second collect never runs, because the first collect never completes
viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) {
    viewModel.uiState.collect(::render)
    viewModel.events.collect(::handleEvent)   // unreachable for a StateFlow
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Two sequential collect calls in one block. The second never starts because StateFlow collection never completes.
  • Calling it in onStart. Each start adds another repeater, so you get N collectors after N trips to the background.
  • Using the Fragment's lifecycleScope/lifecycle instead of viewLifecycleOwner (Q411).
  • Putting one-shot work inside the block. It re-runs on every STARTED (Q420).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. STARTED or RESUMED? → STARTED usually. Visible-but-not-focused (multi-window, a dialog over you) should still render. RESUMED cancels when a permission dialog appears.
  2. In Compose? → collectAsStateWithLifecycle() uses the same idea (F5 chunk).
  3. Is it safe to call from a coroutine not tied to the lifecycle? → It works, but if that outer coroutine outlives the owner you've leaked the outer coroutine, so use the owner's lifecycleScope.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "use it to collect flows safely". The senior answer explains the suspend-until-DESTROYED shape, why multiple collectors need launch, serial execution, the call site and lint rule, and that cancellation is what stops the upstream.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed fragment called repeatOnLifecycle from onStart. After ten trips to the background, each StateFlow emission rendered ten times, and frame drops showed up on the jank dashboard as "only for long sessions".

questions.promptHtml: Fragments have two lifecycles. When must you use viewLifecycleOwner instead of the fragment itself, and what breaks if you don't?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Back-stack bugs are the most common Fragment plus coroutines production issue: duplicate collectors, leaked bindings, null-view crashes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Fragment's own lifecycle runs from onCreate to onDestroy. Its view lifecycle runs from onCreateView to onDestroyView. When you navigate forward with a replace-and-add-to-back-stack, the view is destroyed but the Fragment isn't. If I collect in lifecycleScope from onViewCreated, the old collector keeps running against a dead view. When the user comes back, onViewCreated runs again and adds a second collector. You get duplicate work, leaked bindings, and crashes from touching a null view. Anything that touches views, or is started in onViewCreated, uses viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope and viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle. It's cancelled in onDestroyView and recreated with the next view.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fragment lifecycle:  CREATED ───────────────────────────────────────────── DESTROYED
View lifecycle #1:     [onCreateView ... onDestroyView]   (navigated forward)
View lifecycle #2:                                    [onCreateView ... onDestroyView]  (came back)

lifecycleScope.launch in onViewCreated:  job#1 ──────────────────────────────▶ (until fragment destroyed)
                                                   job#2 ────────────────────▶   ← duplicate
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope:       job#1 ─────┤ cancelled
                                                    job#2 ──────────────┤

Rules:

  • viewLifecycleOwner is valid only between onCreateView (once a non-null view is returned) and onDestroyView. Accessing it outside that window throws IllegalStateException: Can't access the Fragment View's LifecycleOwner when getView() is null.
  • Each new view gets a new viewLifecycleOwner instance. viewLifecycleOwnerLiveData publishes them, which is useful for things created in onCreate that need the current view owner.
  • DialogFragment without a custom view: onCreateView returns null, so there's no view lifecycle owner. Use the fragment's own lifecycle there.

When the fragment's own lifecycleScope is right: non-view work started in onCreate that should last the fragment's lifetime. That's rare, and usually belongs in the ViewModel anyway.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ArticleFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_article) {
    private var binding: FragmentArticleBinding? = null

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        binding = FragmentArticleBinding.bind(view)
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                viewModel.article.collect { binding?.title?.text = it.title }
            }
        }
    }

    override fun onDestroyView() {
        binding = null       // the view-scoped coroutine is already cancelled at this point
        super.onDestroyView()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• lifecycleScope.launch in onViewCreated, the classic duplicate-collector bug (Q419).
  • requireView() or binding!! inside a collector running in the fragment scope, which crashes with NPE/ISE after onDestroyView.
  • Grabbing viewLifecycleOwner in onCreate. It crashes.
  • LiveData's observe(this, ...) in onViewCreated. It's the same bug in LiveData form, and Android Lint flags it (FragmentLiveDataObserve).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. In which order does onDestroyView cancel coroutines relative to your override? → The view lifecycle moves to DESTROYED before onDestroyView() is called, so view-scoped coroutines are already cancelled inside your override.
  2. Compose inside a Fragment? → ComposeView with ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed ties the composition to the view lifecycle, which is the same principle.
  3. Does a Navigation component back-stack entry change this? → The Fragment still loses its view while on the back stack. The NavBackStackEntry is the ViewModelStoreOwner, so ViewModels survive, but views don't.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "use viewLifecycleOwner for views". The senior answer draws both timelines, explains the duplicate-collector mechanism on back navigation, knows the valid window and the exception, and covers the DialogFragment exception and the lint rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team saw NullPointerException on binding in about 0.3% of sessions, all with "navigated back". The collector ran in the Fragment's lifecycleScope and outlived onDestroyView, which had nulled the binding.

questions.subtopic: Choosing scope for work outliving a screen
questions.promptHtml: A user taps "Send" and immediately leaves the screen. Which scopes or mechanisms could run that send, and how do you pick?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the core architecture judgment in this area. Senior candidates map work to its required lifetime and its guarantees instead of defaulting to viewModelScope.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask how long the work must live and what happens if the process dies. If it's fine to cancel when the user leaves (a screen load), use viewModelScope. If it should finish even if the user leaves but can be lost on process death (a short cache write or an analytics flush), launch it in an injected application scope. If it must eventually happen even across process death and reboots (sending a message, an upload), enqueue WorkManager unique work and persist the payload first. If it's user-visible, long-running and must run now (playback, navigation, an ongoing call), use a foreground service with a declared type. The mistake is using one tool for all four.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Need Mechanism Survives leaving screen Survives process death Notes
Screen-bound viewModelScope No No Default for UI data
Finish-in-background, best effort @ApplicationScope scope Yes No Must be short; process can die any time after backgrounding
Guaranteed eventual WorkManager (CoroutineWorker) Yes Yes (persisted in its DB) Constraints, backoff, unique work; not exact timing
Immediate, user-aware, long Foreground service (LifecycleService) Yes No (but less likely killed) Notification required; FGS types required on API 34+
Immediate but guaranteed Expedited WorkManager Yes Yes Quota-limited; runs as an FGS on API < 31

The pattern Google recommends for "start in UI, must not be cancelled by UI" is to have the repository run the work in the external scope and let the caller join/await it:

class MessageRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val dao: MessageDao,
    private val api: ChatApi,
    @ApplicationScope private val externalScope: CoroutineScope,
) {
    suspend fun send(msg: Message) {
        externalScope.launch {           // not cancelled when the caller's scope dies
            dao.insert(msg.copy(state = PENDING))
            api.send(msg)
            dao.markSent(msg.id)
        }.join()                         // caller still suspends until done, while alive
    }
}

If the ViewModel is cleared mid-send, the caller's join() is cancelled but the external job continues. For a chat app I'd go one step further: insert as PENDING locally, then enqueue a unique CoroutineWorker that drains pending messages. That covers process death too.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: the snippet above shows the external-scope pattern. WorkManager is in Q414.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• withContext(NonCancellable) around the whole network call in viewModelScope. It does survive cancellation, but you've lost structure and it still dies with the process.
  • Launching long sync in the app scope "because it's simpler". Android kills cached processes freely, so it gets lost silently.
  • Using a foreground service for deferrable work. Android 12+ restricts starting FGS from the background, and Android 14+ requires a type.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How long does an app-scope coroutine realistically get after the user backgrounds the app? → No guarantee. The process can be frozen by the cached-apps freezer (introduced in Android 11 and enabled by default on many devices in later releases, though OEM-dependent) or killed within seconds under memory pressure. Treat it as "a few seconds, maybe".
  2. Why join() in the repository? → The caller keeps the suspend semantics (spinner, error handling) while it's alive, and the work's lifetime is decoupled from it.
  3. How do you surface the result if the screen is gone? → Persist the state (DB row PENDING to SENT/FAILED) and let any screen observe it. Don't try to call back into a dead ViewModel.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer picks viewModelScope or "use GlobalScope". The senior answer builds the lifetime-and-guarantee matrix, uses the external-scope-plus-join pattern, and moves anything that must happen into persisted WorkManager work.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Chat apps commonly report "message stuck sending" when the send ran in viewModelScope. The fix that sticks is the outbox pattern: a DB row plus unique WorkManager work.

questions.promptHtml: Design an application-level CoroutineScope with Hilt. What goes in its context, how is it injected, and how do you keep it from becoming GlobalScope in disguise?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every serious app has one. Senior candidates get the context right (SupervisorJob, a dispatcher, an exception handler), make it testable, and set usage rules.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I provide a @Singleton scope with a qualifier, @ApplicationScope, in SingletonComponent. Its context is SupervisorJob() so one failure doesn't cancel all app work, an injected default dispatcher (usually Default; callers hop to IO with withContext), a CoroutineExceptionHandler that logs to crash reporting instead of crashing for known non-fatal paths, and a CoroutineName. Classes depend on the qualified CoroutineScope, never create their own, and tests replace it with TestScope/backgroundScope through a test module. The rule for using it: short, idempotent work that should outlive a screen but is fine to lose on process death. Anything that must happen goes to WorkManager.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why each element:

  • SupervisorJob. With a plain Job, the first failing child cancels the scope, and every later launch is cancelled immediately. That's a silent outage for the rest of the process lifetime.
  • Dispatcher injected. It's testable, and Default is a sane base. Don't make it Main: app-scope work isn't UI work.
  • CoroutineExceptionHandler. It's only consulted for root launch coroutines. It doesn't apply to async (exceptions are held in the Deferred) or to children of coroutineScope. Decide deliberately whether a failure here should crash. Swallowing everything hides bugs, so log as non-fatal and rethrow in debug builds.
  • Never cancel it. It lives as long as the process. If someone calls appScope.cancel(), every later launch silently does nothing.
SingletonComponent
 ├─ @DefaultDispatcher CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default
 ├─ @IoDispatcher      CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
 └─ @ApplicationScope  CoroutineScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + default + handler + CoroutineName("app"))
        used by: repositories (external-scope pattern), stateIn for process-wide caches, analytics flush

A legitimate second use is process-wide hot state: someFlow.stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) for a cache shared across screens. Remember that Eagerly in the app scope keeps the upstream alive forever (F5 chunk).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class ApplicationScope
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class DefaultDispatcher

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object CoroutinesModule {
    @Provides @DefaultDispatcher
    fun defaultDispatcher(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default

    @Provides @Singleton @ApplicationScope
    fun appScope(
        @DefaultDispatcher dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher,
        crashReporter: CrashReporter,
    ): CoroutineScope = CoroutineScope(
        SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + CoroutineName("app") +
            CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> crashReporter.recordNonFatal(e) }
    )
}

// Test replacement
@Module @TestInstallIn(components = [SingletonComponent::class], replaces = [CoroutinesModule::class])
object TestCoroutinesModule {
    @Provides @Singleton @ApplicationScope
    fun appScope(testScope: TestScope): CoroutineScope = testScope.backgroundScope
}

(The test module assumes the test graph also provides a TestScope, which is common in Hilt test setups. Adapt it to your harness.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CoroutineScope(Job()) instead of SupervisorJob(). One crash, and the whole app scope is dead until restart.
  • A handler that swallows everything, including real bugs. Combine it with Crashlytics non-fatals and debug-build rethrow.
  • Capturing Activity, Fragment or View references in app-scope lambdas, which leak (Q422).
  • Making it @Singleton without a qualifier, so any CoroutineScope injection gets it by accident.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Could you use ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycleScope instead? → It's tied to the process lifecycle, which never reaches DESTROYED, so it's effectively app-lived. It isn't injectable or testable, and its dispatcher is Main. I prefer the explicit scope.
  2. Should the app scope ever be cancelled? → Not in production. In instrumentation tests, the replacement scope is cancelled per test.
  3. How do you stop teams from abusing it? → Code-review rule plus a custom lint or Detekt check that bans @ApplicationScope injection in UI-layer modules. Document: "short, idempotent, loss-tolerant."

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "make a singleton CoroutineScope with Dispatchers.IO". The senior answer justifies each context element, explains why Job() would be a latent outage, scopes the handler correctly, swaps it in tests, and sets usage governance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app scope built with Job() died after one unexpected JSON exception in a background prefetch. For the rest of that process, cache refreshes silently stopped. The only signal was stale data complaints, until someone found isActive == false in a debug dump.

questions.promptHtml: What is CoroutineWorker, how does it differ from Worker, and what does a correct doWork() look like?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: WorkManager is the standard tool for guaranteed background work. They want the coroutine integration basics: suspend doWork, the dispatcher, the Result types, and cancellation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CoroutineWorker is the Kotlin flavor of WorkManager's worker. doWork() is a suspend function, so I can call suspend APIs directly. It runs on Dispatchers.Default by default, not on WorkManager's configured Executor like Worker. For blocking IO I wrap the code in withContext(Dispatchers.IO), or rely on main-safe suspend APIs. I return Result.success(output), Result.retry() (rescheduled with the request's backoff policy), or Result.failure(). When WorkManager stops the work, the coroutine is cancelled automatically, and cooperative code just unwinds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Persistence. The WorkRequest (input data, constraints, backoff) is stored in WorkManager's internal Room database. It survives process death and reboot, and WorkManager re-runs it when constraints are met.
  • Execution. WorkManager uses JobScheduler on API 23+. It calls your worker and awaits the ListenableFuture that CoroutineWorker bridges to doWork().
  • Dispatcher. The docs say doWork doesn't run on the Configuration executor and defaults to Dispatchers.Default. The old CoroutineWorker.coroutineContext override is deprecated in recent WorkManager versions. Use withContext inside doWork instead.
  • Data limits. Data input and output are capped at 10 KB (Data.MAX_DATA_BYTES). Pass IDs, not payloads.
  • Result semantics. retry() reschedules with exponential or linear backoff (default exponential, 30 s initial, capped at 5 h). failure() ends the chain: dependent work is marked failed too.
enqueueUniqueWork("sync", KEEP, request)
   → WorkManager DB row (ENQUEUED)
   → constraints met → RUNNING → doWork() on Dispatchers.Default
         success → SUCCEEDED | retry → ENQUEUED (+backoff) | failure → FAILED
         stopped (constraints lost / cancel / system) → coroutine cancelled → re-enqueued unless cancelled by you

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class UploadWorker(ctx: Context, params: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, params) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        val id = inputData.getString(KEY_UPLOAD_ID) ?: return Result.failure()
        return try {
            withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { uploader.upload(id) }   // idempotent by id
            Result.success()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            if (runAttemptCount < 5) Result.retry() else Result.failure()
        }
    }
}

val request = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UploadWorker>()
    .setInputData(workDataOf(KEY_UPLOAD_ID to uploadId))
    .setConstraints(Constraints(requiredNetworkType = NetworkType.CONNECTED))
    .setBackoffCriteria(BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .build()
WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniqueWork("upload-$uploadId", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, request)

(uploader is assumed to be provided, for example through a HiltWorker or a custom WorkerFactory.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (e: Exception) that swallows CancellationException and returns retry(). The result is ignored anyway when stopped, but cleanup and logging are wrong.
  • Blocking calls on Default without withContext(IO), which eats a CPU thread.
  • Passing big JSON blobs in Data, which hits the 10 KB limit with IllegalStateException.
  • Non-unique enqueue from onCreate, which duplicates work on every launch.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I report progress? → setProgress(workDataOf(...)) (suspend), observed through getWorkInfoByIdFlow (WorkManager 2.9+) or the LiveData variant.
  2. How do I inject dependencies? → @HiltWorker with @AssistedInject and HiltWorkerFactory, or a custom WorkerFactory.
  3. Periodic work minimum interval? → 15 minutes (PeriodicWorkRequest.MIN_PERIODIC_INTERVAL_MILLIS).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "WorkManager runs background tasks, use CoroutineWorker for suspend". The senior answer covers the dispatcher default, persistence, the backoff defaults, the Data size limit, idempotency, unique work, and the cancellation path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A photo backup worker re-uploaded duplicates after every retry because the upload wasn't idempotent. A server-side idempotency key (the upload ID) fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: When does WorkManager stop a running CoroutineWorker, what happens to the coroutine, and how do you write workers that behave correctly when stopped?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is where WorkManager bugs live: duplicate side effects, half-written files, "work never finishes". It's L3 because it combines cancellation, OS scheduling and idempotency.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A running worker can be stopped because its constraints stopped being met, because the app cancelled it or replaced it with REPLACE, because the system's execution limit hit (JobScheduler gives roughly 10 minutes per run), or because of other system reasons like app standby quotas. CoroutineWorker cancels the doWork coroutine, so the next suspension point throws CancellationException. Any Result you return after being stopped is ignored, and unless the work was cancelled by you, WorkManager reschedules it. So workers must be idempotent and resumable: checkpoint progress, use server idempotency keys, clean up in finally, and never assume one run equals one completion. For runs over about 10 minutes, use setForeground (long-running worker) or split the work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RUNNING ── constraint lost (e.g. Wi-Fi drop) ──▶ onStopped ▶ coroutine cancelled ▶ ENQUEUED (retry later)
        ── cancelWorkById / cancelUniqueWork ─▶ onStopped ▶ cancelled ▶ CANCELLED (no retry)
        ── ~10 min execution limit (JobScheduler) ─▶ onStopped ▶ cancelled ▶ ENQUEUED
