        ── process killed ─────────────────────▶ no callback at all; WorkManager reschedules later

Key points:

  • Stop reason. WorkManager 2.9 added getStopReason() on ListenableWorker (backed by JobScheduler stop reasons on API 31+). Log it, because it explains "why does my sync never finish" in the field. Verify exact constant names against your WorkManager version.
  • Process death is not a cancellation. No finally runs. Your checkpointing must be durable (a DB or file rename), not in memory.
  • CPU loops. A tight parsing loop doesn't suspend, so it ignores cancellation until the next suspension. Call ensureActive() per batch.
  • Retries after stop don't count as failures. runAttemptCount still increments, though. Don't use runAttemptCount alone to give up, or a flaky constraint can exhaust your retry budget.
  • Long-running work. setForeground(ForegroundInfo(...)) promotes the worker to a foreground service (with a notification). On API 34+ you must give a foreground service type and declare it on WorkManager's SystemForegroundService in your manifest. Expedited work on API < 31 also runs as a foreground service and requires overriding getForegroundInfo().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ImportWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        val job = importDao.getJob(inputData.getLong("jobId", -1)) ?: return@withContext Result.failure()
        var offset = job.checkpoint                      // durable checkpoint, resumable
        val tmp = File(applicationContext.cacheDir, "import_${job.id}.part")
        try {
            while (offset < job.total) {
                ensureActive()                           // cooperate between batches
                val batch = api.fetch(job.id, offset, 500)
                importDao.insertAllAndCheckpoint(job.id, batch, offset + batch.size) // one transaction
                offset += batch.size
                setProgress(workDataOf("pct" to offset * 100 / job.total))
            }
            Result.success()
        } catch (e: CancellationException) {
            Log.i("ImportWorker", "stopped, reason=$stopReason at offset=$offset")
            throw e                                      // never swallow
        } finally {
            tmp.delete()                                 // non-suspending cleanup is fine here
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating Result.success() as reached once the work started. Many runs end in a stop.
  • Non-idempotent side effects (payments, "send email") without server dedup keys.
  • Suspending cleanup in finally without withContext(NonCancellable). It throws immediately because the coroutine is cancelled (see the cancellation chunk).
  • Using ExistingWorkPolicy.REPLACE for a long upload triggered on every app start, so it cancels itself forever.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. KEEP versus REPLACE versus APPEND_OR_REPLACE? → KEEP ignores the new request if one is pending or running. REPLACE cancels the existing one, which stops a running worker. APPEND_OR_REPLACE chains after the existing work, or replaces it if that work failed or was cancelled.
  2. How do I test stop behavior? → TestListenableWorkerBuilder to run the worker directly, plus cancelling the coroutine in a test. With WorkManagerTestInitHelper, TestDriver controls constraints and delays.
  3. How does Doze or App Standby affect it? → The job is deferred into maintenance windows, and rarer-bucket apps get fewer runs. Expedited work has a quota (see the Android docs).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "the worker gets cancelled and retried". The senior answer lists the stop causes, separates process death from cancellation, designs checkpointing and idempotency, mentions stop reasons, the attempt-count trap and the long-running/FGS-type requirements.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An import of about 200k rows never completed on low-end devices. Each run hit the 10-minute limit and restarted from zero. Transactional checkpoints per 500-row batch let it finish over three runs.

questions.promptHtml: How do you use coroutines inside an Android Service? What does LifecycleService give you, and what are its pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Services have no built-in scope. The candidate must own cancellation, and know when a service is the right tool at all on modern Android.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A plain Service has no coroutine scope. You either create CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate) and cancel it in onDestroy, or extend LifecycleService from androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-service, which makes the service a LifecycleOwner. Then lifecycleScope is cancelled at onDestroy and repeatOnLifecycle works. Pitfalls: you must call super in the overridden callbacks or lifecycle events don't fire, lifecycleScope runs on Main so heavy work needs withContext, and a running coroutine doesn't keep the process or service alive. On Android 8+ a background service is stopped within minutes, so real long work means a foreground service with a declared type, or WorkManager.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LifecycleService uses a ServiceLifecycleDispatcher to map callbacks to events:

Service callback Lifecycle event dispatched
onCreate ON_CREATE
onStart/onStartCommand, onBind ON_START
onDestroy ON_STOP, then ON_DESTROY

There's no ON_RESUME/ON_PAUSE. So repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) in a service effectively means "from the first start/bind until destroy".

The service lifetime is your job:

  • stopSelf() when the work completes, ideally from the coroutine's completion. Otherwise a started service lingers.
  • If the coroutine fails, still stop the service (try/finally { stopSelf(startId) }).
  • START_STICKY restarts the service after process death with a null intent, and your in-memory coroutine state is gone.

Platform constraints (verify against the target SDK docs):

  • Android 8 (API 26): background execution limits; background startService is restricted.
  • Android 12 (API 31): starting a foreground service from the background is restricted except for listed exemptions.
  • Android 14 (API 34): foregroundServiceType is required, with matching permissions.
  • Android 15 (API 35): dataSync and mediaProcessing FGS types get runtime limits (6 hours within 24 hours for dataSync).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class RecorderService : LifecycleService() {
    override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
        super.onStartCommand(intent, flags, startId)            // required: dispatches ON_START
        startForeground(NOTIF_ID, buildNotification(),
            ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_MICROPHONE)      // API 29+ overload; type required on 34+
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            try {
                recorder.record()                                // suspend, main-safe internally
            } finally {
                stopSelf(startId)
            }
        }
        return START_NOT_STICKY
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting super.onStartCommand/super.onBind, so no ON_START arrives and repeatOnLifecycle never runs.
  • Doing blocking IO directly in lifecycleScope (Main) and causing ANR. A service's onStartCommand runs on the main thread, and service ANR timeouts apply.
  • Assuming the coroutine keeps the service running after stopSelf, or after the system stops a background service.
  • Using a Service for deferrable sync instead of WorkManager.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Bound service: what's the coroutine lifetime? → Until the last client unbinds and the service is destroyed. Clients disconnecting mid-operation cancel nothing unless you design it to.
  2. Can a ViewModel talk to the service? → Through a repository or StateFlow that both share (an app-scoped singleton). Don't hold service references in UI.
  3. ProcessLifecycleOwner versus LifecycleService? → Process lifecycle tells you whether any Activity is foreground. It doesn't make work allowed in the background.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "use LifecycleService and lifecycleScope". The senior answer maps the event table, calls out the super trap, the Main dispatcher, stopSelf in finally, and the API-level FGS restrictions, and knows when to pick WorkManager instead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After targeting API 34, a recording feature crashed with MissingForegroundServiceTypeException on Android 14 devices. The coroutine code was fine. The manifest and startForeground call lacked the FGS type.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to your coroutines, ViewModels and flows on process death, and how do you design so the user doesn't notice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most candidates conflate configuration change with process death. Senior engineers know which state survives which event and design restoration on purpose.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On process death, the OS kills the process without any callback. No onCleared, no onDestroy, no finally blocks, no cancellation. Every coroutine, scope, StateFlow and singleton simply vanishes. When the user returns, Android recreates the task's Activity and Fragment stack from saved instance state, and new ViewModels are created empty. What survives is only what was persisted: the saved-state Bundle (SavedStateHandle, rememberSaveable, navigation arguments), disk (Room, DataStore, files), and WorkManager's persisted work. So I keep small UI-identifying state (IDs, query text, scroll anchor) in SavedStateHandle, re-derive everything else from the database, and route anything that must complete through WorkManager.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Event Activity ViewModel viewModelScope work SavedStateHandle Room/DataStore WorkManager
Rotation Recreated Retained Continues Retained n/a n/a
Back / finish Destroyed Cleared Cancelled Discarded Kept Kept
Process death in background Recreated on return New instance Gone, no cancellation Restored from Bundle Kept Kept, rescheduled
Force stop by user Not restored Gone Gone Discarded Kept Rescheduled on next launch; alarms cleared

Design rules:

  1. Identity in saved state, data in the DB. SavedStateHandle["orderId"] restores the screen, and the ViewModel re-queries Room. savedStateHandle.getStateFlow(key, initial) (lifecycle 2.5+) makes it reactive.
  2. Keep the Bundle small. The saved state goes through Binder, whose transaction buffer is about 1 MB per process and shared by in-flight transactions. A big list causes TransactionTooLargeException (keep it to a few KB).
  3. No in-memory "the previous screen handed me this object". A singleton holder set by screen A is null after restore on screen B. That gives a crash or a blank screen.
  4. In-flight operations. A viewModelScope upload is silently lost. If the user was told "sending...", you need a persisted PENDING state plus WorkManager to finish it, or an honest retry UI.
  5. Hot flows restart cold. A stateIn(Eagerly) cache starts empty again, so the initial value needs to be a sensible "loading" or "restored from DB" state.

How to test: background the app, then adb shell am kill <package> (it only kills a cached or background process), and return via Recents. "Don't keep activities" tests Activity recreation, not process death, because singletons survive it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class OrderViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val savedState: SavedStateHandle,
    repo: OrderRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val orderId: StateFlow<String?> = savedState.getStateFlow("orderId", null)

    val order: StateFlow<OrderUi> = orderId
        .filterNotNull()
        .flatMapLatest { repo.observeOrder(it) }        // re-derived from Room after restore
        .map(::toUi)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), OrderUi.Loading)

    fun select(id: String) { savedState["orderId"] = id }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing only rotation and calling the screen "state-safe".
  • Putting large objects (bitmaps, lists of thousands) in the Bundle.
  • Relying on onCleared/finally for persistence. Neither runs on process death.
  • Assuming a START_STICKY service resumes the coroutine. It restarts the service with a null intent, and coroutine state is lost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does SavedStateHandle survive the user swiping the app away from Recents? → No. Swiping away removes the task, so saved state is discarded. It only covers system-initiated death.
  2. How do you know in the field that process-death restores are happening? → Log when a ViewModel is created with a non-empty SavedStateHandle but an empty in-memory cache. Crashlytics breadcrumbs on "restored" paths.
  3. Why doesn't Kotlin's object survive? → It's a static in the process's class loader. A new process means the class is re-initialized.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "use onSaveInstanceState". The senior answer gives the event-by-state matrix, makes the identity-versus-data split, knows the Binder size limit, covers in-flight work persistence, and knows how to actually reproduce the issue with am kill.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen crashed with lateinit property cart has not been initialized for about 0.5% of sessions on low-RAM devices. The cart came from a singleton populated by the previous screen. After process death, the restored checkout screen had no cart.

questions.promptHtml: A note-editing screen must never lose the user's text: not on back, home, app switch or process death. Where and how do you save, given how Android scopes get cancelled?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It forces you to combine scope lifetimes, lifecycle callbacks, process death and cancellation semantics into one robust design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I don't rely on a single "on leave" moment, because no callback is guaranteed to run before the process dies. First, autosave continuously: each edit updates a StateFlow, and a debounced collector in viewModelScope writes to Room roughly every 500 ms. Second, the current unsaved text goes in SavedStateHandle so process death can restore it. Third, there's a final flush when the user leaves. I trigger it from onStop (or ViewModel onCleared as a synchronous hand-off), and the actual write runs in an injected application scope, so viewModelScope cancellation can't kill it mid-write. onStop is the last callback reliably delivered before the app can be killed in the background, so that's my flush point, not onDestroy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
keystroke ─▶ _draft (StateFlow) ─▶ savedState["draft"] = text     (cheap, survives process death)
                                └▶ debounce(500) ─▶ repo.saveDraft()  (viewModelScope; normal path)
onStop / leaving ─▶ vm.flush() ─▶ appScope.launch { repo.saveDraft(latest) }  (outlives the VM)

Why each callback is or isn't suitable:

  • onDestroy. Not guaranteed when the process is killed in the background.
  • onCleared. Runs on back/finish only, and viewModelScope is already cancelled (Q408). You can synchronously hand the last value to an app-scope coroutine there, but it isn't called on process death.
  • onStop. Called before the app becomes killable in the background on modern Android (onSaveInstanceState is also called around it, after onStop on API 28+). That makes it the best "leaving" hook. It's also called on rotation. A redundant save is cheap if writes are idempotent.
  • Within the coroutine. If the save is in viewModelScope and the user presses back, cancellation can abort a Room write halfway. Room transactions roll back, so you lose the last edit, not consistency.

Making the write cancellation-proof: withContext(NonCancellable) { dao.upsert(draft) } inside viewModelScope does finish, but it delays nothing and stays unowned. The application-scope pattern makes ownership explicit and is testable. Either way, keep it short. Nothing protects against a kill during the write except Room's atomicity.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class EditorViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val savedState: SavedStateHandle,
    private val repo: NotesRepository,
    @ApplicationScope private val appScope: CoroutineScope,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val noteId: Long = checkNotNull(savedState["noteId"])
    val draft: StateFlow<String> = savedState.getStateFlow("draft", "")

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            draft.drop(1).debounce(500).collect { repo.saveDraft(noteId, it) }
        }
    }

    fun onTextChanged(text: String) { savedState["draft"] = text }

    fun flush() {                                  // call from onStop of the host
        val latest = draft.value
        appScope.launch { repo.saveDraft(noteId, latest) }  // not cancelled with the VM
    }
}

(debounce is @FlowPreview in kotlinx.coroutines, so add the opt-in.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving only in onDestroy/onCleared, which never runs on process death.
  • viewModelScope.launch { save() } in onCleared, which is dead on arrival (Q423).
  • Capturing the Fragment or binding in the flush lambda. Capture plain values, like latest above.
  • Writing the full note to SavedStateHandle when it can be megabytes. Cap it, or store only an unsaved delta and the note ID.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why also SavedStateHandle if Room autosaves? → It covers the 0–500 ms debounce window plus process death before a write completed. It's cheap.
  2. Compose version? → The same ViewModel. Call flush() from a LifecycleEventEffect(Lifecycle.Event.ON_STOP) (lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.7+), or a DisposableEffect with a lifecycle observer.
  3. What if saving requires the network? → Save locally first, then enqueue WorkManager unique work to sync. The leave path is never network-bound.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "save in onPause/onStop". The senior answer layers three mechanisms (debounced autosave, saved state, app-scope flush), explains why onCleared and onDestroy fail, and makes the writes idempotent and value-captured.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Support tickets about "lost last sentence" vanished once the final save moved from viewModelScope (cancelled on back) to an app-scoped flush triggered from onStop.

questions.contextHtml:
A list Fragment in a Navigation-based app. QA reports that after opening a detail screen and pressing back three times, each new item update triggers 4 network "mark seen" calls, and Crashlytics shows NullPointerException at binding.recycler in about 0.2% of sessions, all after back navigation. The RecyclerView adapter is fine. Nothing changed in the ViewModel, which a reviewer blamed first.

class InboxFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_inbox) {
    private var _binding: FragmentInboxBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!
    private val vm: InboxViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        _binding = FragmentInboxBinding.bind(view)
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                vm.items.collect { items ->
                    binding.recycler.adapter.let { (it as InboxAdapter).submitList(items) }
                    vm.markSeen(items.firstOrNull()?.id)
                }
            }
        }
    }
    override fun onDestroyView() { _binding = null; super.onDestroyView() }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug(s), explain the mechanism, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a null check on binding" or "move markSeen to the ViewModel init". That hides the crash but leaves N stacked collectors and N network calls. It doesn't explain why the count grows with back navigations.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the Fragment replaced and added to the back stack, or hidden? (Replace means the view is destroyed while the Fragment lives on.) Does the count equal 1 + number of returns? (That confirms stacking.) Is markSeen idempotent server-side? (That sets the blast radius.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Because this is spot-the-bug, ship the scope fix. If it's already in production, make markSeen dedupe by ID in the ViewModel so the duplicate calls stop costing server load.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The collector is in the Fragment's lifecycleScope, so it outlives each view, and each onViewCreated adds one more. (b) repeatOnLifecycle on the Fragment lifecycle. When on the back stack, the Fragment is CREATED (stopped), so collectors pause. When it comes back to STARTED, all stacked repeaters restart together. (c) The ViewModel emits duplicates. This is a red herring, because one collector would show one call.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log System.identityHashCode(this) per collector start. Run the coroutine debug agent (DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines()) after 3 returns and count repeatOnLifecycle children. LeakCanary shows the old binding or view retained by the coroutine lambda.
  5. Root cause: The Fragment lifecycle never reaches DESTROYED while on the back stack, so lifecycleScope and its repeatOnLifecycle survive each view. Every return calls onViewCreated again, which launches another repeater, so after 3 returns there are 4 collectors. They all collect on STARTED, and each calls markSeen. The NPE: between onDestroyView (binding nulled) and Fragment onStop there's a window where a collector can still run against _binding == null. The ordering of the Fragment's ON_STOP relative to onDestroyView during a replace transaction makes that window real.
  6. Fix: short-term: 
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.items.collect { items -> (binding.recycler.adapter as InboxAdapter).submitList(items) }
    }
}
    Long-term: side effects like markSeen don't belong in a UI collector. The ViewModel should derive "seen" from the data stream itself (items.map { it.firstOrNull()?.id }.distinctUntilChanged() collected in viewModelScope), so UI re-subscription never causes duplicate network calls.
  7. Prevention: Android Lint's UnsafeRepeatOnLifecycleDetector warns on repeatOnLifecycle with the Fragment lifecycle (verify it's enabled in your lint baseline). A code-review checklist item: "Fragment + onViewCreated → viewLifecycleOwner". A UI test that navigates back 3 times and asserts one call.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't move the collection to onCreate with the Fragment lifecycle. It fixes stacking but still touches a dead binding. I wouldn't swap _binding!! for ?. alone, because that's silent and the duplicates remain.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if this were Compose inside the Fragment? → Use ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed and collectAsStateWithLifecycle. Same root idea: bind to the view tree's lifecycle.
  • What if the Fragment uses hide()/show() instead of replace? → The view isn't destroyed, so there's no stacking. But STARTED stays true while hidden, so collectors keep running. Use setMaxLifecycle to cap it.
  • Would flowWithLifecycle(lifecycle) have fixed it? → Only if passed viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle and launched in the view scope.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "mark notifications read" endpoint saw 3–6x expected traffic. Every client was one Fragment collector-stack away from multiplying calls. The scope fix plus moving the side effect into the ViewModel cut traffic back to baseline within a release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests null checks or try/catch, can't explain why the call count grows.
  • Hire: identifies the Fragment-versus-view lifecycle mismatch and switches to viewLifecycleOwner.
  • Strong hire: also explains the stacking math (1 + returns), moves the side effect out of the UI collector, and adds lint and a regression test.

questions.contextHtml: You own a 400k-DAU app with about 180 launchWhenStarted/launchWhenResumed call sites. After bumping lifecycle to 2.8.x the deprecation warnings fail the build (allWarningsAsErrors). A teammate opened a PR that mechanically replaces every lifecycleScope.launchWhenStarted { X } with lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { X } }. In the beta channel (5% rollout), three things appeared: an onboarding tooltip shows every time the user returns from Settings, an analytics "screen_view" event count rose 2.4x, and a payment screen started a second startActivityForResult-style launch when returning from the bank app. Crash rate is unchanged at 0.11%, a red herring for "nothing broke".
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, and how would you run this migration safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert and suppress the warning", or "repeatOnLifecycle is the documented replacement so the PR is correct". The first ignores real resource waste. The second misses that the two have different semantics for one-shot blocks.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many call sites collect flows versus run one-shot actions? (That decides the replacement per site.) Are any of the one-shot blocks suspending (delay, awaiting a dialog)? Is there analytics deduplication server-side? (That tells us whether the 2.4x is fully real.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the beta rollout at 5%. To unblock the build, temporarily allow the deprecation via @Suppress("DEPRECATION") on the unconverted sites, without turning off allWarningsAsErrors globally.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Semantics changed. launchWhenStarted ran the block once and paused it while stopped. repeatOnLifecycle re-runs the whole block on every STARTED, so one-shot blocks now repeat on every return from Settings, the bank app, or Recents. (b) Analytics double-counting from the same mechanism. Screen views are logged on each restart. (c) Lifecycle 2.8 itself changed behavior. Unlikely, because the beta diff isolates the PR.
  4. How I'd verify each: Classify all 180 sites with a quick script or grep: body contains collect (restart is wanted) versus not (one-shot). Reproduce the payment case: start the payment, background to the bank app, return, and see two launches in logcat with CoroutineName tags. Compare analytics event IDs per session in beta versus control.
  5. Root cause: A mechanical replacement of pause semantics with restart semantics. Flow collectors benefit (the upstream is cancelled in background), but imperative one-shot work re-executes on every lifecycle re-entry.
  6. Fix: per category: 
    // Collectors → restartable (correct)
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { vm.state.collect(::render) }
}
// One-shot UI action that must wait for STARTED → runs once (lifecycle 2.6+)
lifecycleScope.launch { withStarted { showOnboardingTooltip() } }
// Business one-shots (payment launch, screen_view) → move decision to ViewModel state,
// guarded by a flag in SavedStateHandle so it survives recreation and runs once
    Long-term: screen_view goes to a navigation listener. Payment launch becomes a state-driven, consumed event (see the one-off events chunk).
  7. Prevention: Migrate in batches of about 20 sites per PR, each labeled "collector" or "one-shot". Add a Detekt or custom lint rule banning new launchWhen*. Add an instrumentation test per critical screen that backgrounds and foregrounds and asserts one side effect.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't keep launchWhenX forever. It's deprecated because it keeps upstreams alive in the background. I wouldn't wrap one-shots in repeatOnLifecycle plus an ad-hoc var done = false in the Fragment, which breaks on recreation. withStarted or ViewModel state is cleaner.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• withStarted takes a non-suspending block. What about a suspending one-shot? → Run the suspend work in the ViewModel, and use withStarted only for the final UI step.
  • What if a collector block also had a one-shot analytics.log() before collect? → Split it. The one-shot goes in withStarted or the ViewModel, and the collector stays in repeatOnLifecycle.
  • Does repeatOnLifecycle re-deliver the current StateFlow value on restart? → Yes, a new collector gets the current value, so render must be idempotent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A bulk lifecycle migration doubled a "begin checkout" funnel metric overnight. Product briefly celebrated, until finance noticed revenue was flat. The fix was a per-site classification and moving funnel events to navigation callbacks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves the mechanical PR, or reverts and suppresses forever.
  • Hire: explains pause versus restart semantics and splits collectors from one-shots.
  • Strong hire: adds withStarted and ViewModel-driven one-shots, a staged rollout with classification, lint for new usages, and catches the analytics and payment side effects as the same root cause.

questions.contextHtml:
A marketplace app (1.2M DAU, 60% Android, 35% of devices with 3 GB of RAM or less) lets sellers upload 3–8 photos and then a listing. Since a redesign that added a "Post and keep browsing" button which immediately pops the screen, support tickets about "listing never appeared" jumped from about 20/day to 900/day. Server logs show photo uploads starting but about 18% never completing, with client connections closed mid-body. No crash spike. Crashlytics non-fatal logs show JobCancellationException: Job was cancelled in ListingViewModel.post. One engineer blames a new CDN timeout config deployed the same week.

fun post(draft: Draft) = viewModelScope.launch {
    val urls = draft.photos.map { async(Dispatchers.IO) { api.uploadPhoto(it) } }.awaitAll()
    api.createListing(draft.copy(photoUrls = urls))
}
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose this and redesign the posting flow.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use GlobalScope so it doesn't get cancelled", or "wrap it in NonCancellable". Both survive the screen pop but still die on process death (common on 3 GB devices once backgrounded), have no retry, and give the user no status.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the 18% correlate with the new button versus the old flow that stayed on screen? (That isolates the scope hypothesis from the CDN one.) What fraction of failures happen after app backgrounding? (Process death.) Are uploads idempotent server-side, for example by a client-generated photo ID? Typical upload size and time on p95 networks? (If it's 20 s, it goes beyond any best-effort window.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag the "Post and keep browsing" button off, or make it wait until upload completes with a progress state, while the fix ships. Tell support to ask users to retry.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) viewModelScope is cancelled when the screen pops. JobCancellationException plus the timing of the new button make this most likely. Cancellation propagates to the OkHttp calls, which close the connections, matching the server's mid-body closes. (b) Process death after backgrounding, a secondary contributor on low-RAM devices. (c) The CDN timeout. It would show as server-side timeouts with HTTP status codes, not client-closed connections.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics custom keys for screenPoppedBeforeComplete. Server-side: closed-by-client versus timed-out ratio before and after the CDN change. Locally: tap the button on a throttled network profile and watch OkHttp's EventListener callFailed with IOException: Canceled. For process death, adb shell am kill mid-upload.
  5. Root cause: The work's required lifetime (until the listing is created, even across process death) was bound to a screen's lifetime. The redesign made screen death happen immediately after starting the work.
  6. Fix: short-term: run it in the injected @ApplicationScope with the external-scope pattern. That stops the immediate cancellations, but not process death. Long-term, the outbox pattern: 
    suspend fun post(draft: Draft) {
    val id = listingDao.insertPending(draft)        // durable first; UI shows "Posting..."
    WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueueUniqueWork(
        "post-listing-$id", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP,
        OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<PostListingWorker>()
            .setInputData(workDataOf("id" to id))
            .setConstraints(Constraints(requiredNetworkType = NetworkType.CONNECTED))
            .setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST)
            .build())
}
    The worker uploads each photo with a client-generated ID (idempotent), checkpoints each URL to the DB, creates the listing with an idempotency key, then marks it POSTED. UI everywhere observes the listing row's state. Large batches use setForeground with a progress notification (FGS type dataSync, with Android 14/15 rules).
  7. Prevention: An architecture rule that writes must survive a screen pop and go through the repository, never viewModelScope-owned network writes. A metric for listing time-to-POSTED and the PENDING-older-than-1h count. An instrumentation test that pops the screen mid-upload.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No GlobalScope and no NonCancellable around minutes of network IO. Neither gives retries, persistence, or status. A foreground service alone isn't enough, because there's no persistence across reboot or process death without extra work, and it needs notification UX. WorkManager adds a little latency (scheduling) in exchange for guarantees, and expedited work reduces that.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The user deletes the draft while posting? → Cancel the unique work by name and mark the row CANCELLED. The worker checks the row state between photos.
  • Expedited quota is exhausted? → RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST falls back to regular work. The UI still shows "Posting...", just slower.
  • 10x photos (video)? → Chunked, resumable uploads (server support), with per-chunk checkpoints and a long-running worker.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "fire and keep browsing" UX change turned a correct scope choice into a data-loss bug overnight. The lasting fix wasn't a different scope but an outbox table. After it, "listing never appeared" tickets went back to baseline, and the PENDING-age metric caught two later regressions before support did.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: GlobalScope or NonCancellable, and believes the CDN theory without evidence.
  • Hire: identifies the viewModelScope cancellation and moves the work to app scope or WorkManager.
  • Strong hire: separates screen-pop from process death, uses persist-then-WorkManager with idempotency, checkpoints and observable status, and rules out the red herring with client-close versus timeout data.

questions.contextHtml:
After a release that introduced an injected @ApplicationScope for "background prefetch", the OOM rate on Android rose from 0.04% to 0.21% of sessions, concentrated on 2–3 GB devices and long sessions (over 40 min). LeakCanary in internal builds reports:

┬───
│ GC Root: Thread (DefaultDispatcher-worker-3)
├─ kotlinx.coroutines.internal.DispatchedContinuation
│    ↓ continuation
├─ ProductPrefetcher$prefetch$1 (suspend lambda)
│    ↓ this$0 / L$0
├─ ProductDetailFragment
│    ↓ mView
╰→ androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout  (destroyed view, 2.1 MB retained)

The prefetch code is called from ProductDetailFragment.onViewCreated. It retries fetchRelated() with delay(30_000) backoff up to 10 times. Image cache size was also raised that release, which a reviewer suspects.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the leak, fix it, and say how you'd prevent this class of bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cancel the scope in onDestroy." That's catastrophic. It kills every app-wide job for the rest of the process. Or "Reduce the image cache", which treats the red herring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the prefetch lambda capture: the Fragment, a binding, a callback? Does the leak count grow per product opened? (That points to a per-screen accumulation.) Did the image cache change land in the same build? (It's a confounder, so I'd compare heap dumps by retained type.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-config kill switch for the prefetch, or cap retries to 1 via config. The OOM rate should drop within a day if the hypothesis is right.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The app-scope coroutine captures the Fragment (directly or through a lambda calling a Fragment method), and the 30 s × 10 backoff keeps it alive up to 5 min per product view. That's many detached views in a long session. (b) The bigger image cache raises the baseline heap. Plausible contributor, but LeakCanary's trace points at the coroutine. (c) A Glide or Coil request tied to the Fragment. That's ruled out by the GC root path.
  4. How I'd verify each: The heap dump in Android Studio's Memory Profiler: count ProductDetailFragment instances after opening 20 products. DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() shows about 20 suspended prefetch coroutines in delay. A/B the image cache via remote config separately.
  5. Root cause: Moving work to an application scope changed who owns its lifetime, but the lambda still held a screen-scoped object. this$0 is the Fragment because the call site was appScope.launch { ... binding.related.show(it) ... }, or a callback referencing the Fragment. A suspended coroutine's continuation keeps its captured state strongly reachable from the dispatcher or timer queue until it resumes. Math: about 2.1 MB per view × 20 product views in a 40-min session ≈ 42 MB of retained views, enough to push 2–3 GB devices (with small per-app heaps) into OOM.
  6. Fix: short-term: split responsibilities. The app scope does data-only work and writes results to a repository cache. The UI observes that cache through its own view-lifecycle-scoped collection. 
    class ProductPrefetcher @Inject constructor(
    @ApplicationScope private val appScope: CoroutineScope,
    private val repo: ProductRepository,
) {
    fun prefetch(productId: String) {                  // only plain values cross the boundary
        appScope.launch { repo.prefetchRelated(productId) } // results land in Room/memory cache
    }
}
// Fragment: collect repo.related(productId) with viewLifecycleOwner + repeatOnLifecycle
    Also dedupe by product ID (keep a Map<String, Job> or use a SharedFlow keyed cache) and bound the retries. Long-term: a rule that app-scoped APIs accept only data (IDs, DTOs), never Context, View, Fragment, Activity or lambdas from UI.
  7. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug and QA builds, with failOnLeak in instrumentation tests via LeakCanary's DetectLeaksAfterTestSuccess rule. A Detekt or custom lint rule flagging @ApplicationScope injection in UI modules. Crashlytics OOM rate per release as a release-gate metric.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not appScope.cancel() from a screen. Not WeakReference<Fragment> gymnastics, which works but encodes the wrong ownership. Not moving prefetch back to viewModelScope if it really must outlive the screen. The point is data-only work in the app scope.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob()) per Fragment fix it? → Only if you cancel it in onDestroyView, at which point it's just viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope reinvented.
  • Can the leak happen with viewModelScope? → Yes, if the ViewModel's coroutine captures a View or Fragment. That leaks across rotation, which is a classic.
  • Why didn't the GC collect it? → The suspended continuation is referenced from the scheduled delay task and the Job's children list, which are reachable from the app-scope Job (a GC root via the singleton).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "optimization" that moved prefetch to an app scope cut perceived latency by 200 ms, and quintupled OOMs on low-end devices. Data-only boundaries and a lint check stopped it recurring. The image-cache change, investigated in parallel, turned out neutral.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cancels the app scope in onDestroy, or blames the image cache without evidence.
  • Hire: reads the leak trace, identifies the captured Fragment, and moves UI out of the app-scope lambda.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the retention, gives the data-only boundary rule, dedupes and bounds the retries, adds LeakCanary test gates and lint, and separates the confounder by experiment.

questions.contextHtml:
A "session end" feature: when the user leaves the checkout flow, the app must send a checkout_abandoned event and release a payment SDK session. QA sees the SDK session released, but the server receives the abandonment event for 0% of users. No crash, no log. Analytics dashboard simply shows "no data" for the event since release 7.4.

@HiltViewModel
class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val analytics: AnalyticsRepo,
    private val paymentSdk: PaymentSdk,
) : ViewModel() {

    override fun onCleared() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            analytics.send("checkout_abandoned")   // suspend, network
        }
        paymentSdk.release()                        // plain function
        super.onCleared()
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does the event never arrive, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Network call fails, add retry" or "launch on Dispatchers.IO instead". Changing the dispatcher doesn't help, because the scope itself is dead.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which lifecycle version? (Clearing order matters, Q408.) Is the event fire-and-forget or must it be delivered? Does it matter if the app is killed before it's sent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage, but data loss. Ship a hotfix that sends the event from an app-scoped coroutine, and mark the 7.4 data range as untrustworthy for the analytics team.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) viewModelScope is already cancelled when onCleared() runs, so launch on a cancelled scope creates a coroutine that's cancelled before its body executes. (b) Network failure. That would show retries or errors, and there are none. (c) R8 stripped the call. Unlikely, since the SDK release works.
  4. How I'd verify each: A log line as the first statement in the launched block (it never prints). Check viewModelScope.coroutineContext.job.isCancelled inside onCleared, which is true. A unit test that calls the internal clear and asserts the event.
  5. Root cause: Since the closeables are closed before onCleared() (keyed first, then un-keyed, with viewModelScope among them), the scope's SupervisorJob is cancelled. A launch on a cancelled parent starts in the cancelled state, so the body never runs and no exception is reported (a cancelled launch is silent). paymentSdk.release() works because it's synchronous.
  6. Fix: short-term: make the send independent of the ViewModel. 
    class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val analytics: AnalyticsRepo,
    private val paymentSdk: PaymentSdk,
    @ApplicationScope private val appScope: CoroutineScope,
) : ViewModel() {
    override fun onCleared() {
        appScope.launch { analytics.send("checkout_abandoned") }   // best effort, outlives the VM
        paymentSdk.release()
    }
}
    Long-term: log abandonment from the navigation layer or an onStop flush, because onCleared doesn't run on process death (Q417). The analytics library should queue events to disk.
  7. Prevention: A unit test calling ViewModelStore().clear() (or a test helper) and asserting side effects. Detekt or code review: "no viewModelScope use in onCleared".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not runBlocking in onCleared, which blocks the main thread on a network call and risks an ANR. Not GlobalScope. Not viewModelScope with NonCancellable, since the scope is already cancelled and launch on it won't start.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would withContext(NonCancellable) around the send fix it? → No. launch on a cancelled scope never starts the block, so NonCancellable never gets a chance. It only helps for cleanup inside an already-running coroutine.
  • And on older lifecycle versions? → Same behavior: the scope has been cancelled before onCleared() for the whole viewModelScope history (via the bag-of-tags clear). Don't rely on ordering.
  • What if the event must never be lost? → Write it to an outbox table and let WorkManager deliver it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A funnel metric looked healthy for months because abandonment events never arrived. The "conversion" number was inflated. It surfaced when a data scientist asked why abandonment was exactly zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes the dispatcher or adds retries.
  • Hire: identifies the already-cancelled scope and moves the work to an app scope.
  • Strong hire: also knows onCleared doesn't run on process death, explains silent cancelled-launch behavior, and proposes an outbox for must-deliver events.

questions.contextHtml: A ride-tracking app (900k DAU) polls the driver's location every 5 s while a trip is active. Today a LifecycleService runs the poll in lifecycleScope and the UI binds to it. Product wants the same updates on three surfaces: the trip screen, a home-screen widget (Glance), and the in-app mini banner on other screens. Battery tests show the service polls 100% of the time during a trip, even when the app is in the background with no visible surface, costing about 6% battery per hour. Pressure: ship in 2 weeks, no backend push available yet.
questions.promptHtml: Where should the polling live, who owns its lifecycle, and how do you stop wasting battery?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Keep the service, add a stop button", or "poll in each ViewModel". The first keeps waste and has no reuse across surfaces. The second triples the requests and drifts between surfaces.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must updates continue when no UI is visible (for example, a notification or widget)? What staleness is acceptable (5 s or 30 s)? Is the trip state authoritative on the server, so a missed poll costs nothing? Is a foreground notification already shown during a trip?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Poll only while some surface is visible or a notification/widget needs data, and drop the interval to 15–30 s when nothing is visible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (about the cost): (a) Polling continues with zero observers. (b) Interval is too aggressive for the data's change rate. (c) Radio wake-ups dominate: each poll keeps the cellular radio in a high-power state for several seconds ("radio tail"), so 5 s polling effectively holds it on. This usually matters more than CPU.
  4. How I'd verify each: Battery Historian and Perfetto traces for radio activity. The Android Studio Energy Profiler. A/B on a 20-device cohort for 1 hour, comparing batterystats.
  5. Design: one TripTracker singleton in the data layer exposes StateFlow<TripState>, built with stateIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(10_000), Loading). The poll loop is the upstream, so it runs only while someone collects. The UI surfaces collect with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) or collectAsStateWithLifecycle. Every surface shares one upstream. A foreground-service notification (if product wants it visible when backgrounded) is just another subscriber: it collects the same flow in its own scope. 
    @Singleton
class TripTracker @Inject constructor(
    api: TripApi, @ApplicationScope appScope: CoroutineScope, visibility: AppVisibility,
) {
    val state: StateFlow<TripState> = flow {
        while (true) {
            emit(TripState.Active(api.driverLocation()))   // main-safe suspend
            delay(if (visibility.isForeground.value) 5_000 else 30_000)
        }
    }.stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(10_000), TripState.Loading)
}
    (Error handling is omitted for brevity. Add retryWhen and catch non-cancellation errors, see the error-handling chunk.)
  6. Fix timeline: Week 1: the shared singleton flow, replacing the three pollers. Week 2: adaptive intervals plus a notification subscriber. Later: push (FCM or WebSocket) replaces polling entirely, and TripTracker internals change but its API doesn't.
  7. Prevention: An energy dashboard metric (battery per active-trip hour), and a test with fake time that verifies the upstream stops 10 s after the last subscriber leaves.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: App scope plus WhileSubscribed avoids a long-lived service for the data path. But a widget update with no subscriber needs an explicit trigger: WorkManager periodic work has a 15 min minimum, so a widget needing 5 s freshness is an unrealistic requirement I'd push back on. Do not use Eagerly, which polls forever.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Widget process: does it share the singleton? → Glance widgets update from the same process (WorkManager or a receiver), but it may be cold-started. The widget should read the last cached state from DataStore or Room, not expect the live flow.
  • Two trips at once? → Key the flow by trip ID (a Map<TripId, StateFlow> with ref-counting), because stateIn inside a function creates a new upstream per call (F5 chunk).
  • Network error loops? → Exponential backoff in retryWhen, and a surfaced Stale state after N failures.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A tracking screen shipped with a poller per view. A busy afternoon turned 3 pollers per user into a 3x load spike on the location endpoint. A shared WhileSubscribed flow cut requests by two thirds and removed the drift between the banner and the map.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: per-ViewModel polling, or a service that never stops.
  • Hire: single shared upstream with lifecycle-driven start and stop.
  • Strong hire: reasons about radio tail energy, adaptive intervals, widget limits, the push migration path, and measures with Battery Historian.

questions.contextHtml: A news app (3M DAU) schedules a "refresh feed" PeriodicWorkRequest every 15 minutes with CoroutineWorker, plus an additional appScope.launch { while (true) { refresh(); delay(60_000) } } started in Application.onCreate "to keep it fresh". Play Console vitals show the app in the "excessive wake-ups" bucket, and p90 background battery draw is 2.1x the category median. 41% of refreshes return identical content (304 or same ETag). The server team complains about 3M × 60 requests/hour peak. Another red herring: image prefetch is only 5% of the radio time.
questions.promptHtml: What would you change, and how would you justify the numbers to the team?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the delay to 5 minutes" without touching the design, or "delete the WorkManager job". Neither addresses the double scheduling or the lifecycle of the loop.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What's the freshness SLA for background versus foreground? Does the backend support ETags or If-Modified-Since? Do we have push (FCM) for breaking news? What share of users are active versus idle?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-config the loop off (or interval to 10 min) without a release. That alone removes up to 60 requests per user-hour.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The while(true) loop in app scope runs for the entire process lifetime, which includes background, and wakes the CPU and radio constantly. The process stays warm because it keeps getting work. (b) The periodic worker's 15-minute floor is redundant with the loop. (c) 41% redundant refreshes show missing conditional requests.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto and Battery Historian for wake lock and radio timelines. adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler and dumpsys batterystats. Server logs: requests per user-hour by client version. The coroutine dump shows a single long-lived loop coroutine.
  5. Root cause: An unbounded app-scope loop with no visibility awareness, layered on top of WorkManager. Both do the same job, so redundancy costs energy and requests while adding no freshness when the app isn't in use.
  6. Fix:
    • Foreground freshness: refresh in a repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) collector or WhileSubscribed upstream, so it runs only while visible (about every 60 s, with jitter).
    • Background freshness: only the periodic worker (15 min minimum), with Constraints(requiredNetworkType = CONNECTED) and setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true). For breaking news, FCM data messages trigger an expedited OneTimeWorkRequest.
    • Conditional requests: send If-None-Match. A 304 costs a few hundred bytes instead of a full body, and skips parse and DB writes.
    • Add ±20% jitter so 3M clients don't hit the server on the same minute boundaries.
    // Foreground-only loop, in a flow that disappears with the last subscriber
val freshFeed = flow {
    while (true) { emit(repo.refreshIfChanged()); delay(60_000) }
}.stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), FeedState.Idle)
    Math: if 20% of 3M users are active in the foreground at peak, requests drop from 3M × 60 = 180M/hour to 0.6M × 60 = 36M/hour, plus background 3M × 4 = 12M/hour, about 48M/hour total, roughly a 73% cut. With 41% of those becoming 304s, the bytes saved are larger still.
  7. Prevention: An energy budget in CI (a Macrobenchmark or a battery test device farm), Play vitals alerts, and a code-review rule: no unbounded loops in app scope without a visibility gate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use exact alarms or a foreground service to "guarantee" freshness, which is a policy and battery problem. Slightly staler background content is fine because the first foreground refresh fixes it in under a second.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product insists on 1-minute background freshness? → Only with push. Polling at that rate in background isn't permitted by the platform's design, and Doze defers it anyway.
  • Does WorkManager periodic guarantee exactly every 15 min? → No. It's the minimum interval, with a flex window, and it's deferred by Doze and standby buckets.
  • How to confirm the savings? → Staged rollout by percentage with a holdout, comparing Play vitals wake-ups and server request counts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "keep fresh" loop added in a hurry ran for two years. Removing it shifted nothing in engagement metrics, and the app dropped out of the excessive-wake-ups list the next release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the delay only.
  • Hire: removes the always-on loop and keeps visibility-gated foreground refresh plus WorkManager background.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the request savings, adds conditional requests and jitter, uses push for urgency, and validates with an experiment.

questions.contextHtml:
A PM asks: "When the user opens the Promo screen, show a 10-second countdown, then auto-navigate to the offer. If they rotate, it shouldn't restart or skip. If they leave and come back, it should restart." Current implementation, in an Activity:

lifecycleScope.launch {
    for (i in 10 downTo 1) { binding.timer.text = "$i"; delay(1_000) }
    startActivity(Intent(this@PromoActivity, OfferActivity::class.java))
}

Observed: rotating restarts the countdown at 10 (about 31% of sessions have a rotation, since the screen is used on tablets), backgrounding to answer a call then returning triggers a navigation while the app is in the background on some devices, and one tester saw the offer opened twice.
questions.promptHtml: Clarify the requirement, then redesign it so the behavior is correct and testable.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Save the counter in onSaveInstanceState." That fixes rotation only, still navigates from the background, and doesn't handle double navigation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should the clock keep running while the app is in the background, or pause? If the app is backgrounded for 8 seconds and returns, do we navigate immediately, or give the user the remaining time? Is the countdown the absolute 10 s from first shown (wall clock), or active screen time? What if the user taps "skip"? Should it survive process death?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Since the behavior is ambiguous, I'd propose a default: the countdown pauses when not visible, resumes on return, survives rotation, restarts after the screen is left and re-entered, and navigation fires once and only while visible. I'd confirm with the PM before building.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for the observed bugs): (a) The coroutine is in the Activity lifecycleScope, destroyed and re-launched on rotation. State is local to the coroutine. (b) lifecycleScope doesn't pause on STOPPED, so the loop finishes in the background and startActivity runs there, subject to background-activity-start restrictions on Android 10+. (c) Double navigation on rotation timing: the old coroutine finishes right as the new one starts, or two launches happen.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the coroutine start with the Activity's identity hash across rotations. Background with adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_HOME mid-countdown and watch logcat. A fake clock in tests.
  5. Root cause: UI-timeline state (the remaining seconds) lives in a UI-owned scope and a local variable, and the side effect (navigate) isn't tied to visibility or consumed once.
  6. Fix: The ViewModel owns the countdown and exposes state. The UI renders it, and navigation is a consumed state. 
    class PromoViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(PromoUi(seconds = 10, navigate = false))
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()
    private var ticker: Job? = null

    fun onVisible() {                        // called from repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) start
        if (ticker?.isActive == true) return
        ticker = viewModelScope.launch {
            while (_state.value.seconds > 0) {
                delay(1_000)
                _state.update { it.copy(seconds = it.seconds - 1) }
            }
            _state.update { it.copy(navigate = true) }
        }
    }
    fun onHidden() { ticker?.cancel() }      // pause: remaining seconds stay in state
    fun onNavigationHandled() { _state.update { it.copy(navigate = false) } }
}
    The UI (repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)): call vm.onVisible(), try { collect } finally { vm.onHidden() }; when navigate is true, navigate then call onNavigationHandled(). The ViewModel survives rotation, so no restart. Leaving the screen clears the ViewModel, so the next entry restarts. The navigate flag is only observed while STARTED, so no background navigation. Consuming it prevents duplicates. Process death: a restored screen starts fresh from 10, which matches "restart after leaving".
  7. Prevention: A runTest test using advanceTimeBy(3_000), simulating hidden/visible, and asserting seconds and a single navigation. A lint or review rule against startActivity inside bare lifecycleScope.launch.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't compute from System.currentTimeMillis() unless the PM wants wall-clock semantics. It would navigate immediately after a long background, which may surprise users. I wouldn't keep the loop in the Activity and just save an Int, because the other two bugs remain.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PM changes to "wall-clock 10 s, don't pause"? → Store a deadline (SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() + 10_000) in the ViewModel (and SavedStateHandle for process death), derive remaining time on each tick, and navigate on return if past due.
  • Compose version? → Same ViewModel, with collectAsStateWithLifecycle and LifecycleStartEffect for onVisible/onHidden.
  • Why viewModelScope and not lifecycleScope with state in a ViewModel? → The ticker's pause/resume logic is business behavior, so it's testable and rotation-proof in the ViewModel.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "redirect after 5 seconds" timer in a Fragment opened a payment screen on top of a phone call overlay. Moving the timer to a ViewModel with visibility gating and a consumed navigation flag fixed it, and the clarifying question about backgrounding would have saved the original bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: saves the counter in the Bundle and ships.
  • Hire: moves the timer to the ViewModel and gates navigation on visibility.
  • Strong hire: asks the pause-versus-wall-clock question first, makes navigation a consumed state, handles process death deliberately, and tests with virtual time.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review for a 6-hour incident: after release 9.2, "lateinit property userSession has not been initialized" crashes hit 1.4% of sessions (about 38k/day), concentrated on devices with 3 GB of RAM and less, and only for users returning from background after 10+ minutes. Crash stack:

Fatal Exception: kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException:
  lateinit property userSession has not been initialized
    at com.app.account.AccountViewModel.loadProfile(AccountViewModel.kt:41)
    at com.app.account.AccountFragment$onViewCreated$1.invokeSuspend(AccountFragment.kt:58)

userSession was set by LoginViewModel into an @Singleton SessionHolder after login. 9.2 added "Account" as a deep-link entry point. The timeline: crash started when 9.2 reached 20%, the on-call first suspected a bad coroutines-library bump in the same release (it was exactly that, version 1.8 to 1.10), and rolled it back at hour 3 with no effect. At hour 5 someone reproduced it using adb shell am kill.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review: root cause, why detection was slow, what to fix and what process changes to make.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the property nullable and return early." That removes the crash but leaves users on a blank or logged-out screen, and misses why the holder was empty and why the on-call chased the wrong cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask (in the review): What changed in 9.2 besides the library bump? (The deep link.) What does the device/OS/RAM distribution of crashes look like, and does time-in-background correlate? Did our QA matrix include a process-death test? Where is the session persisted?
  2. Immediate mitigation (what we should have done by hour 1): Gate the deep-link entry through a splash that restores the session (or fall back to login if missing), and ship it behind a remote-config flag. Halt the rollout at 20%.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (and why the first was wrong): (a) Process death: the symptom (low RAM, long background, cold re-creation straight into Account) screams it. (b) The library bump: a red herring that caused a 3-hour detour, because a rollback of an unrelated change can't fix a state bug, and nobody validated the hypothesis before acting. (c) The deep link bypassing the normal launcher flow where the session is initialized.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crash reports segmented by ActivityManager.isLowRamDevice, process start reason (ApplicationExitInfo with REASON_LOW_MEMORY on API 30+), and time since background. Reproduce: open Account, background, adb shell am kill com.app, return from Recents. An instrumentation test doing the same through ActivityScenario.recreate() is not enough, as it doesn't kill the process.
  5. Root cause: In-memory singleton state (SessionHolder) was treated as an invariant. After process death, Android restored the Activity stack straight into AccountFragment (and the new deep-link route also bypassed the launcher), but Application.onCreate and the splash flow that normally rebuilt the session didn't run in that path. A lateinit hid the nullable reality until access. Classic: the code assumed "screen A always ran before screen B".
  6. Fix: short-term: the Account screen obtains the session through a suspend sessionRepository.requireSession() that reads the encrypted persisted token and restores it (or navigates to login), never through a lateinit populated by another screen. Long-term: session state is persisted (EncryptedSharedPreferences/DataStore) and exposed as a StateFlow<Session?> initialized in Application or the DI graph on first access. Screens depend on the repository, not on the previous screen's side effects. ViewModels load via IDs in SavedStateHandle (Q417). 
    class AccountViewModel @Inject constructor(private val sessions: SessionRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val profile = sessions.session                      // StateFlow<Session?> restored from DataStore
        .flatMapLatest { s -> if (s == null) flowOf(ProfileUi.LoggedOut) else repo.profile(s.userId) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProfileUi.Loading)
}
  7. Prevention: A process-death CI test (instrumented: launch a screen, am kill, relaunch via the task). A lint/Detekt rule discouraging lateinit on cross-screen holders. A review checklist: "does this screen work if it is the first thing created in a new process?" Release gate: crash-free sessions by RAM bucket at each rollout stage (1%, 5%, 20%) with automatic halt. An incident-practice rule: before rolling back, state the hypothesis and the evidence that would confirm it.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not nullable-and-ignore. Not "Don't keep activities" as the only test, which keeps singletons alive. Not rolling back unrelated changes on a hunch. Persisting a session carries a security cost (token at rest), so encrypt it and keep the TTL honest.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How does a coroutine in viewModelScope relate? → It died with the process too. Nothing in the coroutines library caused this. The restored ViewModel was new and its coroutine began from empty state.
  • Could SavedStateHandle hold the session? → Only a user ID, never a token. Tokens belong in secure storage.
  • How would you detect similar issues proactively? → Log "cold process, non-launcher entry" events and compare crash rates between launcher and restored-entry paths.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An incident ran 6 hours because the team trusted the correlation with a library bump. The review's biggest win wasn't the code fix but a rule: reproduce or find a distinguishing signal (device RAM, time in background) before rolling back.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: makes the property nullable, or blames the coroutines upgrade.
  • Hire: identifies process death and a singleton assumption, and persists or restores the session.
  • Strong hire: adds process-death reproduction in CI, RAM-bucketed rollout gates, a "first screen in a new process" checklist, and a process lesson on validating hypotheses before rollbacks.
